full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—These two appeals by special leave are directed against a common judgment of the High Court Division dated 16 February 1983 disposing of Second Appeals Nos. 402 and 403 of 1971, They arise respectively from title Suit No. 532 of 1967 and Title Suit No 87 of 1969 of she 1st Court of Munsif, Sylhet. In one suit, M.S. No. 532 of 1967. a simple declaratory decree was sought to the effect that a sale-deed dated 9-9-59 purportedly executed by the respondent was viol, and in the ether suit, T.S No. 87 of 1969, recipient of the sale-deed namely, the appellant prayed for establishment of her title on the basis of the said sale-deed. The sale-deed has been held 'void' all-through. Facts leading to these appeals are briefly given below.

2. In T.S. No. 533 of 1967, plaintiff-respondent, Faizun Nessa Chowdhury, an old widow, alleged that the husband or defendant-appellant. Sufia Khanam, came to her house accompanied by a relation, Dabiruddin and requested her to veil the suit land to Sufia Khanam whereupon an agreement was reached for sale of the land for a consideration of Tk. 2,000/-, that on the following evening, at Magreb prayer time, she was taken to the house of Dabiruddin where she was paid Tk. 200/- as earnest money and she was requested to give her left thumb-impressions on a blank sheet of paper which was intended to be the required bainapatra. Accordingly, she put her on the blank paper believing that she was executing a bainapatra but after some time a Sub-Registrar came to enquire from her about the matter and asked her to admit execution of a sale-deed. She denied having executed any sale-deed but explained that she had executed a bainapatra by putting her L.T.I. on a blank paper in view of this denial the Sub-Registrar refused registration of the sale-deed whereupon an appeal was preferred which was also dismissed. There-upon the defendant filed a suit. T.S. No. 73 of 1962, under section 77 of the Registration Act which was decreed on contest and the sale-deed was registered on 6 March 1963. The plaintiff then filet this suit, T.S. No. 532 of 1969, for a declaration that the sale-deed was void being brought about by fraud, collusion and misrepresentation. Defendant Sufia Khanam then filed the other suit, T.S. No. 87 of 1967. for declaration of her title and recovery of possession of the suit land on the basis of the sale-deed registered in pursuance of her decree passed in T.S. No. 73 of 1962. as referred to above. Both the suits were tried analogously by the learned Munsif who dismissed suit No. 87 of 1969 end decreed suit No. 532 of 1967 on a finding that the sale-deed was Iliad having been insisting about by fraud and collusion. This decree was challenged in two separate; appeals which were also dismissed by as learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment dated 8 September 1970 whereupon the decree was challenged in two second appeals, namely S.A. No. 402 of 1971 and S.A. No. 403 of 1971. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division after hearing the matters together dismissed the appeals but directed the plaintiff of T S. No. 532 of 1967 to amend her plaint within two months so as to include a prayer for cancellation of the document failing which, it was further directed, her suit would stand dismissed and that of the defendant Sufia Khanam, would stand decreed.

3. Leave has been granted to consider : (i) whether the learned Single Judge is well-founded in law in directing amendment of the plaint of respondent's suit No. 532 of 1967 with a view to include a prayer for cancellation of the document after having held that her suit for mere declaration is not maintainable In the absence of a prayer for consequential relief ; (ii) whether the cancellation of a document is a consequential relief or further relief under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or it is an independent relief which cannot be available to the plaintiff except by a separate suit under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act ; (iii) whether the proposed amendment will change the character of the suit and its cause of action; and (iv) whether such amendment if allowed will militate against the law of limitation.

4. Mr. MH Khandkar, learned Counsel for the appellant, contends that the suit for declaration of nullity of the sale-deed in question being surely a suit for declaration, according to the plaintiff herself, it was liable to be dismissed when the learned Single Judge found that it was not maintainable in the absence of a prayer for further or consequential relief. This argument does not appear to be tenable, for even if the prayer for further relief was no included in the plaint the Court got power to direct amendment of the plaint so as to Include such a prayer at any stage of the proceedings if the court considers such amendment to be necessary it the interest of justice. The learned Single Judge is found to have rightly relied upon the decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Keramat Ali vs. Md. Yunus. 15 DLR SC 120 and the Indian Supreme Court in the case of A. K. Gupta and Sons Ltd V. Damodar Valley Corporation, AIR 1967 (SC) 96.  In the Indian case it was held that the only condition for amendment of the plaint is that it will not take the defendant by surprise by introduction of new case or any new cause of action altogether or it will not change the character of the suit. As to limitation, though the law of limitation is to be followed in the matter of amendment, but in appropriate cases the rigidity may be relaxed and amendment may be allowed even after the expiry of the period of limitation. But in the instant case the question of amendment of the plaint as directed by the learned Single Judge will not be of much importance in view of other facts and circumstances which are going to be discussed presently.

<u>5. Mr. M.H. Khondkar has contended that the relief by cancellation of a sale deed is not a consequential relief but it is an "independent relief" which can be available only by a separate suit. On this point the learned Counsel's stand appears to be inconsistent with the arguments advanced on behalf of the appellant before the High Court Division where it was argued that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of prayer for consequential relief", that is, relief by cancellation of the document. Be that as it may, the main question now is whether toe relief of cancellation is a consequential relief or an independent relief. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act does pot specifically provide for cancellation of a document but it Is section 39 of the Ace which specifically provides for cancellation of any written instrument" which includes both a deed of transfer and a decree. Section 39 provides for declaration of nullity of a written instrument in the words 'adjudge it so" void it also provides that the court 'in its discretion' may order the instrument, when adjudged void, to be delivered tip or cancelled. Front the provision it is obvious that the declaration of nullity is the main and substantive relief. whereas cancellation of the instrument is a consequential relief.</u>

<u>6. In a Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Kalu Ram V. Balm Lal AIR 1932 All. 485 (FB)=ILR 54 All. 812, Sulaman, C.J. observed that the cancellation of a document is much more than a declaratory relief; that it is a substantive relief and that ad-valorem court-fee will be necessary for such a relief under section 7 (iv)(c) of the Court-fines Act. Fat is of that case were quite distinguishable and in view of a number of reliefs having been prayed for In that suit, which was for both declaration and cancellation, this view was expressed as an obiter; but two out of the five Judges constituting the Full Bench did not fully share this view of Sulaiman, C.J. In a subsequent case. Sri krishan Chancka V. Mahabir Prashad ILR 55, All. 791 another Full Bench of the same High Court consisting, among others, of three Judges who were members of the Full Bench in Babu Lal's case, held that a suit for mere declaration that an instrument was void was quite maintainable without a prayer for the relief of cancellation. It appears that the wordings of these two sections 39 and 42, are such as to create some confusion in a casual mind about the nature of reliefs contemplated therein when a suit is brought for declaration of nullity and, or for cancellation of any written instrument. For better appreciation both the sections are quoted below:</u>

<u>"39. Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable, and the Court may in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.</u>

<u>If the instrument has been registered under the Registration Act, 1908, the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation."</u>

<u>"42. Any person entitled to any legal character, or 10 any right as to any properly, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion made therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief;</u>

<u>Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff. being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so.</u>

<u>7. It appears that relief by declaration of nullity of any instrument and also relief by cancellation of the instrument have been specifically provided for in section 39, Specific Relief Act. This section appears in Chapter V which opens with the words OF THE CA N. CELLATWN OF INSTRUMENTS. Section 42 appears in Chapter VI which opens with the words OF DECLARATORY DECREES. Section 42 does not specifically provide for declaration of nullity of any written instrument  nevertheless, a decree for nullity of any Instrument comes in under this section in view of the general provision therein as to declaration of any legal character as expressed in the words "any person entitled to any legal character". If by an instrument a person's light and title is clouded or threatened. he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected or that any other person who denies his title or claims title in himself has not acquired any right or title thereby. If the suit is filed for a declaration that a written instrument, whether it is a sale-deed or a court's decree, "is void", it clearly comes under section 39, since it is covered by the expression "any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable ..... may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable". But if a further prayer is included in the suit that by the void instrument the plaintiff's right has not been affected, then this prayer comes straight under section 42; similarly, if this prayer is framed in a different form, that is, the defendant acquired no right or interest thereby, it will make no difference, for this prayer is also covered by section 42. If his suit includes the relief's that the instrument in question is void and his right has not been affected thereby and, or, the defendant acquired no right thereby, then the reliefs are covered by both sections 39 and 42. In such cases provisions of sections 39 and 42 will over-lap.</u>

<u>8. A similar question was exhaustively dealt with in a Full Bench decision in the case of Duibaki Lal Vs. Iqbal Ahmed, (1965) 17 DLR, 119, Sattar, J. one of the there learned Judges constitution the Full Bench has observed that if the provisions of these two sections 39 and 42 are read together it win be seen that they overlap each other and in (Some cases it may be difficult to express any definite opinion as to whether it falls exclusively under section 39 or section 42 and that there is hardly any difference between a prayer to adjudge a document void or voidable and a prayer for declaration that the document is so, Keeping in. view the language and terms in which the first part of each of these two section has been expressed namely, the part relating to a mere declaration of nullity of R document. we have no hesitation to hold that a snit far declaration that the instrument is void and that it has not affected the plaintiff's right or the defendant has not acquired any right thereby is a suit falling under both the sections. Even if some auxiliary reliefs ale added to the plaint, such as the document has been brought about by fraud, forgery and false personation, still the suit will retain its character as a suit for mere declaration. This is what s has exactly been held in the case of Daibaki Lal in which a number of reliefs have been held to be mere declaratory reliefs, namely, that the instruments in question are void, that the defendant has acquired no interest in the suit property by the instruments, that these Instruments have been brought into existence by forgery and false personation and that no consideration passed by the said instruments.</u>

<u>9. The question which is of fundamental importance in the case before us is whether a relief byway of cancellation of a. written instrument is one which must be given by the court after it declares it void whether of Hot such relief has been specifically prayed for. The next question is whether such relief should be given by the court even if it has not been paid for that is advalorem court fee has not 'been paid under section 7(iv)(c) of the Court-fees Act Mr. MH, Khondkar has read section 39 so as to find therein the relief by cancellation of a document to be an integral part of the decree of nullity of the document. In other word s, he is of the view that ill a suit under section 39 mere declaratory decree cannot be passed without granting the relief of cancellation of the document. Divergent views on this point have been expressed and in some cases extreme views have been taken. In the case of Katia Pillai and another Vs, Ramashami Piilai and others, AIR 1929 Mad 393, a Division Beach of the Madras High Court after finding that a will produced by the defendant was a forged one observed that as the Will was void it was the function of the court to order cancellation of the Will as a part of the decree. In some cases it has been observed that though the court should grant the relief of cancellation it cannot do so unless there is a prayer to that effect and ad-valorem court fee is paid for it. In some other cases it has been hold that even if there has been " no specific prayer for cancellation of the instrument but nature of the plaint is such as to imply a prayer for cancellation, then the court should grant this relief provided it has been paid for, obviously by necessary amendment of the plaint. On this point two out of three Judges constituting the Full Bench in the case of Daibaki Lal, as referred to above, appear to have held slightly divergent views. Hasan, J. has observed that the court is not bound to give relief for cancellation of a document in every case under section 39 whether there is a prayer for cancellation or Hat, that language of section 39 does not make it obligatory on the court to order cancellation of the document even if it is prayed for, and that this relief may be granted only when. it is prayed for and not otherwise. Sattar J. observed that it depends upon the facts of the case, that the relief of cancellation need not he specifically asked for in view of the language of section 39, that in determining whether in a suit cancellation has been asked for, the plaint should be read as a whole and the court will not "confine itself  merely to the form of the plaint but it must look to the substance of the relief claimed" and that if on consideration of the plaint the court comes to the conclusion that 'both declaration and cancellation have been intended then the court must grant both provided required court fee is paid. Regarding payment of court fee according to the value of the relief claimed all the three Judges, third Judge being Sayem, J. were unanimous that for cancellation of an instrument court fee must be paid under section 7 (iv)(c) of the Court- fees Act.</u>

<u>10. Considering the language of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act in the light of the Full Bench decision in Daibaki Lal’s case, which, we find, gave correct exposition of the law, we are of the view that in a suit under this section the plaintiff may seek merely a decree tor nullity of the instrument which is the main and substantive relief, bus if he prays for its cancellation also which is consequential relief, then he will have to pay for it. But cancellation of the instrument is not indispensably necessary in all cases. Tile court is also not required to grant the relief of cancellation whenever it adjudges the instrument void though the plaintiff seeks its cancellation, for both the reliefs of declaration of nullity and cancellation are within discretion of the court.</u>

<u>11. The next question is in which case the court must insist on cancellation of the instrument after it is declared void or voidable. Consistent views of superior courts including the Privy Council are that a void document need not be cancelled. Cancellation of an instrument declared void is unnecessary when the plaintiffs possession in the land, when it is the subject mutter of the instrument. is undisputed or established. The Privy Council in the case of Petherpermal Vs. Munlandi Serdac, ILR 35 Cal. 551, observed that it was unnecessary fur the plaintiff to have a deed set aside as H was void and inoperative and that the suit was governed by Article 144 and not Article 99 of the Limitation Act. In the Full Bench decision in Daibaki Lal's case. Sayem J. observed that if the plaintiff is a party to the instrument the court refuses, as a rule, to grant such a declaratory relief, on the ground that the instrument, in such a case, need be avoided by cancellation, The plaintiff in such a case is required to pray for cancellation, by way of a consequential relief; where, however, the plaintiff is not party to the instrument no such difficulty arises.</u>

<u>12. It may be pointed out that the reference to the Fun Bench did not include any term for consideration of the question of cancellation on the basis or whether a plaintiff was party to it or not. Rather. one of the terms (No.2) precisely one of the terms in Daibaki's case was whether it is necessary for the plaintiff in a suit for declaration as to a document being void ab-initio to ask for consequential relief as contemplated under section 39 and if be has not specifically asked for such a relief, whether he should be held, by necessary implication, that there is a prayer for such a relief, because it comes under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. The answer given is no. We take the view that the answer was given correctly and like to add further that where the document is ex-facie void its cancellation is not necessary even if the plaintiff is a party to it Mr.M,H. Khondkar has contended that a written instrument whether it is a deed Of a decree, is an insurmountable obstruction to the plaintiff's getting his title declared and relying on a decision in the case of V. Koner Vs.R, Konar , AIR 1939 Mad, 894, contended that no declaratory decree can be granted unless such obstruction is removed first. This obstruction may be removed by a declaration that the instrument is "void into", as has been held in that very decision.</u>

<u>13. In the instant case before us there is a clear finding of both the courts below as well as the High Court Division that the instrument is void in that it has not been executed by the plaintiff  respondent as a sale-deed. In view of this finding the direction for amendment of the plaint in order to include a prayer for cancellation of the document was not necessary. The learned Single Judge of High Court Division has relied upon the decision in 6 DLR 254 and 21 DLR 6261 without looking into the facts of these cases. which are Kanchanmala Bepari Vs. A.K. Bepari and Mono Mohini Devi Vs. S.A. Bhuiyan respectively, Facts of these cases are not similar to that of the instant case. The learned Single Judge did not refer to the Daibaki Lal's case The learned Single Judge treated the instant suit as one under section 42, Specific Relief Act, and observed that in the absence of a prayer for the farther relief, that is, for cancellation of the instrument, it is not maintainable. The suit is found to be falling under both the sections, 39 and 42. In a suit under section 39, where relief of cancellation is found necessary by the court but it has not been prayed for. the suit cannot be dismissed but the court will require the plaintiff to pay additional court fee for the relief of cancellation. In a suit under section 42, where consequential relief is found necessary but has not been prayed for the court may either dismiss the suit Of direct the plaintiff to pay additional court fee for the purpose keeping in view the general principle that a document which Is void, ab-initio need not be cancelled. If a written instrument is adjudged void and it is further declared that it has not affected the plaintiff's right it need not be cancelled, The declaratory decree that the document is void and plaintiff's right has not been affected thereby will give him adequate relief, Of course in view of this declaratory decree the instrument will not stand cancelled but will remain on record. In his own interest therefore the plaintiff should also seek the additional relief by way of setting aside the decree or cancelling the deed, Section 42 as has been pointed out above does not specifically provide for declaration of nullity and cancellation of a written instrument, but section 39 does so. In section 39, two kinds of documents have been referred to one is 'void' and the other in 'voidable'. Where a document has been adjudged voidable it win have to be avoided both by declaration and cancellation: and if the document is adjudged void or void ab-initio it need not be cancelled.</u>

<u>14. In view of what has been discussed above we hold that the impugned sale-deed which has been held void by the court because of fraud need not be cancelled and that the direction for amending the plaint for the purpose of cancellation of the document is unnecessary.</u>

15. In the result, the judgment and decree of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division is modified to the extent that the direction for amendment of the plaint is set aside and that of the trial Court is restored. With this modification the appeals are dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J : Judgment-debtor(defendant No. 4) is the petitioner. She is challenging an order of the High Court Division dated 3 September 1986 setting aside an order of the Exevuting Court, namely the Subordinate Judge, who had directed the appointment of an Advocate Commissioner to ascertain the value of a part of her building for payment of compensation to her by the decree holders who were liven decree for khas possession over a land including this part of the building. Respondents obtained a preliminary decree in her portion suit (O.C. Sot No. 52 of 1972) for a saham of .13 decimals of land out of a total area of 31 decimals. The preliminary decree was made final on 9.8.84 upon an Advocate Commissioner's report which was made part of the decree. By that final decree the respondents were allotted the saham of .13 decimals and it was directed that they would be given khas possession of the land including a part of the judgment debtor’s building. When the decree was sought to be put into execution in O.C. Execution Case No. 5 of 1984, the judgment-debtor objected to the execution contending that the value of the part of her building should be ascertained through an Advocate Commissioner for the purpose of compensation to be paid by the decree-holders. The Executing Court allowed her prayer and appointed an Advocate Commissioner; but in revision the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division (Civil Revision No. 229 of 1986, Rangpur Bench), set aside the order of the Executing Court and directed that the Execution Proceeding should proceed. This order of the High Court Division is now under challenge before us.

2. Mr. Abdul Malek learned Advocate for the petitioner, first of all tried to show us that the judgment debtor’s petition for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner by the Executing Court is maintainable under section 151 C.P.C. The learned Counsel has tried to argue that as there is no other provision of law for ascertainment of value of a part of the building which fell to the decree-holders' share, provisions of section 151 C.P.C. are applicable. We do not think that this contention is tenable. For, remedy sought in the application goes into the merit of the decree itself in which rights and liabilities of the parties have been conclusively determined.  Under this decree, decree-holders are not liable to pay any compensation for demolition of a part of the building which fell to their saham. Function of the Executing Court is strictly limited to execution of the decree as it is. It appears that after the preliminary decree was passed an Advocate Commissioner appointed by the Court made local investigation but the judgment debtor did not co-operate with him, that the Advocate Commissioner gave the plaintiffs a saham of .13 decimals including a part of the judgment-debtor's building and a latrine since these structures fell within the plaintiffs' saham of .13 decimals out of which .4 decimals of land was found in possession of the defendant-judgment-debtor. The Advocate Commissioner submitted his report which was accepted and made part of the final decree without any objection. In the circumstances, the Executing Court got no authority to go beyond the decree and award compensation to the judgment-debtor who is however at liberty to remove her structure taking permission of the Executing Court.

<u>3. The learned Counsel has tried to invoke section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act and contended that as a transferee the judgment-debtor is entitled to compensation for demolition of her building constructed bonfire in a land which, subsequent to her transfer, became property of another person. Facts established in the suit however do not appear to sups a bonfire transferee. Out of the total area of .31 decimals of the suit land, which had belonged to defendant No. 5, plaintiffs first purchased .13 decimals and after them defendants Nos. 1-3 purchased imams leaving only .06 decimals which was purchased, last of all, by defendant No. 4 the judgment debtor. Now it is found that he is in unauthorized 26 (State) possession of .4 decimals out of the plaintiffs 13 decimals and it is this part of land under unauthorized possession of .4 decimals on which the disputed constructions were made. The construction is, therefore, not bonafide. In any case, to ascertain value of the part of the judgment-debtor's building so as to compensate him at plaintiffs' cost falls outside the power of the Executing Court and as such the order appointing an Advocate Commissioner has been rightly set aside by the High Court Division. We find nothing to interfere.</u>

The petition is dismissed.

End.

This Rule is against the judgment and order of reversal passed by the Subordinate Judge.

2. The opposite party No. 1 filed on 27th January, 1978 Pre-emption Case No. 16 of 1979 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in respect of certain land on the allegations, inter alia, that he was a co-sharer in the holding by inheritance and he had no knowledge about the transfer of the land under pre-emption to purchasers—the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, before me. The petitioners resisted the said case by filing joint written objection. Their case was that the case under section 96 of SAT Act was barred by limitation and they were benamder of his father Lal Mahmud who was a co-sharer in the holding in possession.

3. The trial Court dismissed the case on contest on 20.7.82. The pre-emptor's Miscellaneous Appeal No. 382 of 1982 against the judgment and order of the trial Court was allowed.

4. Mr. Abu Sayeed Ahmed submits that the learned Subordinate Judge upon a wrong interpretation of the decision in the case of Ashwini Kumar Karmaker Vs. Hari Mohan and others 35 DLR (AD) 334 and the case of S Joga Moya Debi and others Vs. SDD Singh Hazari and others 36 DLR 272 set aside the judgment and order of the Trial Court. He also cites the case of Yakub Khan and others Vs. Amjad Ali and others 27 DLR 164 to contend that in a summary proceeding under section 96 of the SAT Act Court cannot look into the question of benami. He contends that in view of the decree made in Title Suit No. 153 of 1978 declaring the title of Lal Mahmood in the land under pre-emption the lower appellate Court committed an error in law in allowing the pre-emption case inasmuch as at the time of judgment and order passed by the lower appellate Court in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 382 of 1982 the petitioners had no title in the land under pre-emption and the lower appellate Court committed an error of law in deciding the question of benami in pre-emption proceeding. He also contends that the pre-emptor was not a necessary party in the said Title Suit and as such the court of appeal below took a wrong view that the decree made in the Title Suit No. 159 of 1978 is not binding on the pre-emptor-opposite party inasmuch as an ex parte decree is as good as a contested decree.

<u>5. From perusal of the judgments of the courts below it appears that the pre-emption case was filed prior to the institution of the Title Suit by Lal Mahmud against the petitioners before me for declaration that they were his benamdcr and he was the real purchaser of the land under pre-emption. He obtained an ex parte decree in the suit in a hot haste on 7.12.78 within 3 months of its institution. But the pre-emption case although filed earlier was rejected on 20.7.82. In the case of Yakub Ali the pre-emption case was filed on 2.6.68 and the vendor of the land in that case contested the pre-emption case on the ground that there was an agreement for re-conveyance between him and the purchaser and he filed Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 on 15.6.67 for specific performance of contract and obtained an ex parte decree on 12.3.66. On facts the decision is distinguishable. In that case unlike the instant case there was an agreement for re-conveyance and the transfer was subject to that condition. Therefore, in my opinion, the principle laid down in that case has no manner of application to the facts in the present case. The learned Advocate also relied on the decision in the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Bibran Chandra Das 51 CWN 644 and the case of S Joga Moya Debi and others Vs. SDD Singh Hazari 36 DLR 272 in support of his contention that in a pre-emption case the court cannot examine the benami nature of transaction. He also cited the case of Upendra Vs. Janab Ali, 29 DLR 229. None of the cases cited has relevancy to the instant case. From the judgment impugned before me it appears that the learned Judge while allowing the Miscellaneous Case found that the Title Suit No. 159 of 1978 was filed after 7 months of filing the pre-emption case and plaintiff, Lal Mahmud obtained the ex parte decree against the party Nos. 1 and 2 within 3 months of the institution of the suit, that appellant before him was not impleaded in the title suit as a party to whom a statutory right of pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act accrues and the decree was a collusive one and was not binding upon the opposite party No. 1 pre-emptor. Thus, it appears that the lower appellate Court did not enter into the question of benami transaction; rather it proceeded on the ground that the ex parte decree passed in the Title Suit was obtained collusively without impleading the pre-emptor in the suit although the pre-emption case was filed earlier to the institution of the Title Suit. The contention that as at the time of disposal of the pre-emption case there being no subsisting title to the pre-emptees under the kabala in view of the decree made in the Title Suit instituted by Lal Mahmud the pre-emption case is not maintainable is misconceived as it has been found and, according to me correctly, by the appellate Court that the decree made in Title Suit is not binding upon the pre-emptor as he was not made party to the said Title Suit. Where during pendency of a pre-emption case under section 96 of the SAT Act a decree is passed in a suit where the pre-emptor is not impleaded as party the decree made in that suit does not defeat the right of the pre-emptor accrued to him under section 96 of the SAT Act to pre-empt the land. The decision in the case of Meher Abjar Vs. Jalal Ahmed Howlader, 13 DLR 642 supports this view of mine. In the instant case the appellate Court did not proceed to examine the question of benami and as such the decisions cited in this case on behalf of the petitioners have no manner of application.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Ansar Ali, J.: This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner calls in question the judgment and order dated 19.12.85 passed by Mr. TK Rudra, Senior Munsif, Sadar, Mymensingh in Miscellaneous Case No. 325 of 1981 allowing an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and setting aside an ex parte decree dated 29.10.81 passed in Other Suit No. 510 of 1981 and restoring the said suit to its file and number.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule in a nutshell are as follows:

The petitioner as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid Other Suit No. 510 of 1981 on 1.9.81 against the defendant-opposite party and another for ejectment of the principal defendant-opposite party No. 1 from a portion of the suit premises in which he had been in possession for a long time as a licensee of co-defendant-opposite party No. 2. It is the case of the plaintiff-petitioner that the disputed holding covered by CS Khatian No. 219 of Mymensingh town belonged to one Azit Sheikh who died leaving a son Newaz Ali and four daughters. The original owner sold the suit-holding by kabala dated 20.6.42 to one Hiran Prava Sarker and Lakshmi Bala Debi and while in possession they defaulted in payment of rents. Hence the landlord instituted a suit against them and obtained a rent decree in 1949 and the said decree was put into execution in Execution Case No. 22 of 1950 and ultimately the suit holding was auction sold  execution of the decree to one Azmat Ali, father of pro-defendant opposite party No. 2 on 14.3.1950 and the said sale was confirmed on 5.5.50 and the auction purchaser took delivery of possession of the suit holding through court on 15.7.51.

3. During the liberation war in 1971 the defendant-opposite party No. 1, full-brother of the auction purchaser late Ajmat Ali came over to Mymensingh with his family from Saidpur and started residing in some portion of the disputed holding with permission of said Ajmat Ali. Thereafter in the month of January, 1980 the Pro-defendant No. 2 asked defendant No. 1 to vacate the suit premises but the defendant No. 1 refused to vacate the same. Meanwhile, the heirs of the auction purchaser late Ajmat Ali sold out the suit holding by two kabalas dated 11.6.81 to the plaintiff-petitioner who thereafter asked the defendant No. 1 to vacate the suit holding but without any result, hence the suit for ejectment of defendant- opposite party No. 1 from the suit holding.

4. It has been stated in the instant revisional application of the plaintiff-petitioner that on 10.9.81 summons was duly served upon the defendants one by receiving acknowledgment of service from pro-defendant No. 2 and other by hanging a copy of the summons on the fencing of the but of the defendant opposite party No. 1 as he refused to receive the same. It is the further case of the plaintiff-petitioner that in spite of the service of summons, none of the defendants entered appearance to contest the suit; hence the same was taken up for hearing ex parte on 29.10.81. Accordingly the learned Munsif examined the plaintiff-petitioner on oath and admitted into evidence some documents filed by the plaintiff and thereafter on consideration of the same decreed the suit ex parte and directed the eviction of defendant-opposite party No. 1 from the suit-holding. Thereafter the plaintiff-decree-holder put the decree into execution by Execution Case No. 14 of 1981 and the decree was executed through court on 26.11.81 with eviction of defendant-opposite party No. 1 from the suit-holding. Then on 28.11.81 the judgment debtor opposite party No. 1 filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex parte decree and restoring the suit to its file and number on the ground of non-service of summons upon him. The said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 325 of 1981 in the Second Court of Munsif, Sadar, Mymensingh. The plaintiff-petitioner contested the said Miscellaneous case by filing a written objection on 28.4.83. The defendant-petitioner of tile Miscellaneous case who is opposite party No. 1 in this revision case examined himself as PW 1 and another Kalu Sheikh a neighbour as PW 2 in support of his case. The plaintiff-opposite party of the said Miscellaneous case who is the present petitioner also examined himself as OPW 1 and the Process server one Jamal Ahmed as OPW 2 in support of his case. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties and on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record came to a finding that the summons in Other Class Suit No. 510 of 1981 was not duly served upon defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case, that is the present opposite party No. 1 and allowed the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on contest, set aside the ex parte decree dated 29.10.81 and restored the original suit to its original file and number of condition of payment of a sum of Tk. 100.00 to the contesting plaintiff opposite party of the Miscellaneous case by the defendant-petitioner within 15.1.86 vide judgment and order dated 19.12.85.

5. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff as petitioner moved an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure in this court and obtained the present rule.

6. Mr. SR Karmaker, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner, seriously assailed the judgment and order of the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge, mainly on the ground that the learned Munsif came to a wrong finding upon misconception of law and facts to the effect that the summons was suppressed and not duly served upon the defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case and illegally set aside the impugned ex parte decree and restored the suit to its file and number and as a result there has been a failure of justice. His next contention is that in the instant suit, service of summons was duly effected in full compliance of rule 17 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon the defendant- petitioner of the Miscellaneous case, but he did not turn up to contest the suit, Hence it was rightly decreed ex parte. Further contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that in a case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the onus is upon the defendant-petitioner to prove that summons was not duly served upon him, but in the instant case, he has failed to discharge that onus, on the other hand, the plaintiff-opposite party of the Miscellaneous case has been able to discharge his onus to prove that the summons was duly served upon the defendants, particularly defendant No. 1 by hanging, as he refused to receive the same. To prove the service of summons, the plaintiff examined himself as OPW 1 and the process-server as OPW 2 who of course admittedly was a colleague of the plaintiff. Hence, the impugned judgment and order of the learned Munsif setting aside the ex parte decree and restoring the suit to its file and number is wholly bad, illegal and liable to be set aside.

7. It appears that a vokalatnama was filed for the defendant opposite party No. 1 in this case by one Mr. AHM Ziauddin, Advocate, but at the hearing of the rule none appeared for the opposite party. However I have heard the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner at length, perused the impugned judgment and order along with the evidence and other materials on record and considered the submissions of the learned Advocate in support of this Rule. Admittedly it is the case of the plaintiff-petitioner that service of summons in the instant suit was effected upon defendant No. 1 in accordance with the provisions of rule 17 of Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure which are as follows

"17. Procedure when defendant refused to accept service or cannot be found where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgment, or where the serving officer, after using a due and reasonable diligence cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed."

8. From the certified copy of the service-return of the process-server, it appears that he had gone to the addresses of the defendants at 88 and 61 Purhit Para, Mymensingh town, Kotwali, PS Mymensingh respectively and found both the defendants. Defendant No. 2 received the summons with acknowledgment, but defendant No. 1 the petitioner of the Miscellaneous case refused to receive the same by giving any acknowledgment. Hence the process server served the summons by hanging a copy of the same upon the fencing of the homestead of defendant No. 1 on 10.9.81 in presence of some mokabila witnesses namely Mukter Hussain, Abdul Mannan, Murmoz Mia and defendant No. 2 Quddus, but this service-return was challenged by defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case alleging it to be false and concocted one, as the defendant No. 1, the present opposite party was not at all present in his house on 10.9.81 and there was no question of his refusal of the summons. The alleged service of summons by hanging on the outer door of his house or on the fencing of his dwelling but or on any conspicuous part of the same in presence of the witnesses as mentioned in the so-called service-return was not genuine. The process-server being a colleague of the plaintiff-petitioner was in collusion with him and he falsely submitted the service return with false statement therein. The learned Munsif could not rely on the evidence of OPW 2 the process server and the so-called service-return. He rather relied on the deposition of PW 1 the defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case and that of PW 2 Kala Mia who deposed to the effect that no notice of Other Class Suit No. 510 of 1981 was served upon the defendants. The defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case came to know about the original suit only on 26.11.81 and that he was in possession of the suit-holding but an attempt was made to dispossess him therefrom on 26.11.81 in execution of the decree in his absence and thereafter he instituted the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 28.11.81. It appears that he stated while deposing in cross examination by mistake that he received the summons but at once he corrected himself saying that he did not receive the summons. PW 2 Ka Sheikh in his evidence stated that he was a neighbor of the defendants and there was no service of summons of the original suit upon the defendants and the process server did not visit the suit-holding for service of summons. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record came to a finding that no service of summons was duly made upon the defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case and accordingly allowed the Miscellaneous case and set aside the ex parte decree and restored that suit to its file and number. It is true that the initial onus is upon the defendant-petitioner to prove non-service of summons upon him in a case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case, it appears that the initial onus was fully discharged by the defendant by his evidence of denial of service of the summons in any manner and that of PW 2 by corroborating him and thereafter the onus was shifted upon the plaintiff-opposite party of the Miscellaneous case to prove due and proper service of the summons upon the defendant-petitioner. The plaintiff of course, in discharge of his onus examined himself as OPW 1 and the process server as OPW 2. Therefore it appears that there is no fault in respect of the discharge of respective onus by either of the parties and the learned Munsif on due consideration of the evidence of both the sides and other materials on record believed the case of non-service of summons upon the defendant-petitioner of the Miscellaneous case and disbelieved the case of due service of summons of the plaintiff-opposite party of the said case and came to a definite finding that the summons in the instant suit was not duly served upon the defendant petitioner of the Miscellaneous case and accordingly allowed the Miscellaneous Case. I myself have also scrutinized the materials on record and I find no illegality in the said finding of the learned Munsif which is a finding of fact based upon proper consideration of the evidence on record.

9. It may be further noted that "the affixation of the copy on the outer door is not an idle ceremony, nor it is an immaterial part of the service. Its object is to give due publicity to the act of the process-server and to impress the party that formal service is being effected. Rule 17 itself shows its importance. The report of the process-server must show the affixation, and the persons in whose presence it was done. The cardinal fact and important matter of rule 17 is affixation of the copy. If rule 17 provides for a mode of service, the affixation itself is the service or at least the most essential part of the service. It as observed in a decision in the case of Ganeshmal Vs. Kesoram Cotton Mills Ltd. reported in 55 CWN page 349 (355). In the instant case, it appears that the process server named in his alleged service return at least 3 persons as mokabila witnesses, but none of them has been produced in court by the present plaintiff-petitioner as witness to prove the service of summons by hanging a copy of the same on the outer door on any conspicuous part of the house of the defendant No. 1. This also raises a doubt as to the genuineness of the service of summons upon defendant No. 1 by the process server.

<u>10. Thus from the above, I am of the view that the learned Munsif very correctly found that there was no due service of summons of the suit upon the defendant No.1 and he rightly set aside the ex parte decree and restored the suit to its file and number. The finding as to non-service of summons is a finding of fact and this cannot be interfered with in revision by this court, unless the same is perverse or not based on any evidence. Hence I find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

<u>The impugned judgment and order does not suffer from any illegality and there has been no failure of justice. The same is therefore upheld. The rule is accordingly discharged but without any order as to costs. The order of stay is vacated. Let the suit be proceeded with expeditiously. Communicate this order to the court concerned.</u>

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and order dt. 6.4.86 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 652 of 1985.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This is plaintiffs appeal by special leave. He obtained an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No.3b8 of 1980 and got delivery of possession of the land in suit in execution of the decree. But on an application filed by the defendant respondent under Order IX, rule 13, Civil P.C., the decree was set aside and the suit was restored to file subject to payment of Tk. 500/- as adjournment cost to the plaintiff. He challenged this order by a revision application, under section 115 of the Civil P.C., before the High Court Division, which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by order dated 6 April, 1986.

<u>2. Leave was granted by us to consider the question whether the trial Court which, having been satisfied that the summons was duly served upon the defendant recorded a finding to this effect and passed the decree, has, thereafter, got power to go against its own finding and set aside the ex-parte decree when the defendant did not appear before the Court to depose on oath that the summons was not served upon him.</u>

3. The suit was filed in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka by the appellant for declaration of title to 'A' schedule land and recovery of possession in 'B' schedule land, which is a part of schedule 'A', as shown in his plaint. Case of the appellant is that when the process server went to the house of the respondent to serve the summons the latter refused to accept it whereupon the Process server served the summons by hanging it at the gate of the respondent in presence of witnesses and there after he submitted his report with a declaration that he had served the notice upon the defendant. The learned Subordinate Judge on perusal of the service return, along with the declaration of the process server, recorded a finding that he was satisfied that the summons was duly served and on the finding decreed the suit ex-parte by an order dated 13 June 1984. Appellant put the decree into execution and got delivery of possession of the land through the court on 5th April 1985. Thereupon the respondent filed an application under Order IX, C.P.C. for setting aside the decree taking the ground that no summons was served upon him, but it was fraudulently suppressed and that he came to know about the suit and the decree therein for the first time when the decree was executed through court. The appellant filed a written objection denying the allegation that the summons was fraudulently suppressed and asserted that it was duly served and, in support of his contention he deposed as a witness in the court. He was cross examined on behalf of the defendant but the defendant did not depose in the court in support of his contention that no summons was served upon him. The learned Subordinate Judge on these materials passed the impugned order on 25 April 1985 allowing the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree with an observation that in his opinion summons was not duly served and that for ends of justice the defendant should be given a chance to contest the suit". This order was challenged in revision Civil Revision No. 652 of 1985- but the rule issued thereon was discharged by the learned Single Judge.

4. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, has seriously assailed the order setting aside the ex-parte decree. He has contended that there was no material whatever before the court to set aside the ex-parte decree by altering its own finding that the summons was duly served. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has relied upon a number of decisions. On the other hand, Mr. AJ. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate for the respondent has contended that the trial court which had passed the ex-parte decree got ample jurisdiction to reverse it if it was satisfied on consideration of the application of the defendant that no summons was served upon him; in support of this contention the learned Advocate also cited a number of cases. Most of the decisions cited by both the learned Counsels are found to have been referred to, in the judgment of the High Court Division.

5. It appears that the impugned decision of the learned Single Judge has been mainly based on a decision of this Court in the case of Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet V. Israil Ali and others, 1981 BSCR, 222. In that case this Court held that a court while passing an ex-parte decree must be satisfied that all requirements of law have been fulfilled and held that the decree passed in that case " neither satisfied the legal requirements, nor from such finding the alleged case of the plaintiff was proved." We are constrained to observe that this decision as relied upon by the learned Single Judge has been misprice acted and misapplied in the instant case by him as this decision got no relevance in the instant case. Facts of that case are very much different from those of the instant case. Here, in the instant case, the question is non-service of summons upon the defendant, but in that case there was no such question as the defendant was admittedly served with the summons and he also entered appearance but did not file written statement on the date fixed for the purpose and nobody was present nor any steps taken when the suit was taken up for hearing. The plaintiff in that case was examined and some "rent receipts were also admitted in evidence and on these materials the plaintiffs claim of tenancy-right under the Government-defendant was declared. The defendant's application under Order IX, rule 13, C.P.C. was rejected by the trial Court as well as the revisional court whereupon the matter was brought before this Court by special leave. It was found that the plaintiff who was lessee of the Government till 1956 claimed tenancy right and filed the suit in 1968 for a declaration to this effect. In these circumstances, this Court held that even in a case of ex-parte decree the court passing the decree must be satisfied that the legal requirement for passing a decree have been fulfilled. Secondly, this Court found that on the date the defendant was found absent the exparte decree was not passed by the trial Court as the court fee paid by the plaintiff was found insufficient; to enable the plaintiff to put in the deficit court fee an adjournment for one month was given to him by the trial Court; but when the defendant filed an application to submit written statement his application was refused and the ex-parte decree was passed. This decision therefore does not help the respondent of the instant case.

6. The learned Single Judge has gone into the question as to onus of proof in the case of an application for setting aside an ex-parte decree. It appears that the learned Single Judge accepted the contention of the respondent that it was not for him (defendant) to adduce that the summons was not served upon him but it was for the plaintiff to show that the summons was duly served. There is no dispute that the onus to prove that the summons was duly served upon the defendant is on the plaintiff. In this case this onus is found to have been fully discharged as the process-server submitted his report, along with a declaration, that he has served the summons by hanging it on the gate of the defendant when the latter refused to accept it and thereafter the plaintiff appeared in the court and deposed on oath that the summons was duly served. Thereupon the onus shifted upon the defendant to prove that the summons was not served as claimed by the plaintiff and it was incumbent upon the defendant to depose on oath that no summons was served upon him by the process server as alleged. The process server was, of course, not examined as a witness as his examination is not mandatory in view of the provision of rule 19A of Order V, Civil P. C. Examination of the process server is mandatory when he has simply submitted his report about the service of summons without any verification or declaration that he had served the summons, but when he made a declaration to this effect then his examination as a witness is not mandatory, although the court may at its discretion call him as a witness. This question as to examination of the process server when the summons is served under rules 17 and 19 of Order V, has been decided by this Court in the cases of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty and others v. Motaleb Hossain and others, 36 DLR (AD) 248=1985 BLD (AD) 59 and Khurshed Anwar v. Jamil Akhter, 1982 BLD (AD) 83.

7. Mr. AJ. Mohammad Ali has tried to show us that when the trial court arrived at a finding that the summons was not served duly, the High Court Division rightly refused to interfere therewith in revision. But the question is what is the basis of trial court's finding that the summons was not served. The basis, as appears from record, is the mere claim of the defendant made in his application under Order IX, rule 13 C.P.C. that no summons was served upon him. This claim was not backed by him by adducing evidence in court as against the process server's report and the evidence of the plaintiff. As such this claim is not sufficient for the trial court to alter its previous finding that the summons was duly served. In the circumstances the trial Court is found to have illegally set aside the ex parte decree; the learned Single Judge did not direct his attention to this aspect of the matter.

8. In the result, the appeal is allowed; the impugned orders of the High Court Division and the trial Court are set aside and the application under Order IX, rule 13,C.P.C. is dismissed. No order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
The rule which arose out of the application for condonation of delay in preferring appeal was heard by the Bench comprising Mr. Justice Bimalendu Bikesh Roy Choudhury and Mr. Justice Abdul Hasib and as their Lordships failed to return an unanimous verdict, their Lordships entered into dissenting judgment. It is under these circumstances that the matter was placed before the learned Chief Justice for passing an appropriate order and the learned Chief Justice has referred this matter to this Bench for disposal.

2. Facts involved in the case do not admit of any dispute. Plaintiffs who figured as opposite parties in Civil Rule brought a suit against the petitioner and others seeking declaration of their title in respect of certain land described in the schedule of the plaint. The suit was decreed on 23.9.89. On 1.10.89 an application was filed on behalf of petitioner for certified copy of judgment and decree which were made ready and taken delivery on 17.10.89. A proposal for preferring an appeal was made on 19.11.89 and the same was sent to the learned Deputy Solicitor who on scrutiny of the papers forwarded the matter to the office of the learned Deputy Attorney-General (Civil) and it was received by said office on 1.1.90. The learned Deputy Attorney-General then endorsed the matter to the learned Assistant Attorney-General (Civil) who, received it on 6.1.90 and prepared the memo of appeal on 7.1.90. But in the meantime prescribed period for filing appeal expired on 4.1.90. Petitioner presented the memo of appeal in the filing section of the Court on 10.1.90. But the memo of appeal though out of time by 6 days was not accompanied with application for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act. The stamp reporter on scrutiny found that the memo of appeal was out of time by 6 days and returned the same to the filing Assistant Attorney-General on 21.1.90.

3. After a lapse of one month, the matter was referred to the Deputy Solicitor with the opinion that no useful purpose would be served in filing the appeal in as much as it has no merit and there is no material on record in support of petitioner's case. This was done on 20.2.90. On 18.3.90 the Deputy Solicitor opined that the appeal should be filed and referred the matter to the learned Attorney General on 4.4.90 for opinion. On the same day the file was sent to the office of Solicitor. The learned Attorney General received back the file there from on 18.4.90. On the following day he sent back the same to the office of the Deputy Solicitor with an opinion to file the appeal. The file was received back by the learned Assistant Attorney-General on 21.4.90. Since the Court remained closed from 22.4.90 to 10.5.90 and that the learned Assistant Attorney General was away from the station, so delay occurred in preparing the application for condonation of delay. Thereafter petitioner filed the application in Court together with memo of appeal seeking condonation of delay of 6 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act contending that delay was caused due to reasons which were, "unintentional, accidental and beyond the control of the petitioner."

4. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that file moved from one office to another in the matter of securing opinion and in this process this delay of 6 days occurred. It is further submitted that the Court remained closed from 22.4.90 to 10.5.90 and that the Assistant Attorney-General was away from station, so delay occurred in preparing the application for condonation of delay. Thereafter petitioner filed the application in Court together with memo of appeal seeking condonation of delay of 6 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act contending that the delay was caused due to reasons which were "unintentional, accidental and beyond the control of the petitioner." It is further contended on behalf of the petitioner that because of movement of file from one section to another section and as there was "a difference" of opinion as to whether appeal should be filed or not, this delay occurred.

5. The learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite parties submits that the appeal had been filed on 4.1.90 for which Deputy Solicitor made over necessary papers to the learned Deputy Attorney General (Civil) on 1.1.90. But the memo of appeal was presented in Filing Section of the Court on 10.1.90. Although the prescribed period for filing appeal had run out in the meantime. It is further submitted that within the knowledge of the learned Assistant Attorney-General period of limitation in presenting the appeal having run out, the memo of appeal was not accompanied by application seeking condonation of delay. So the petitioner acted with gross negligence and carelessness. It is further submitted that there was want of due diligence, inasmuch as that memo of appeal was submitted before the stamp reporter who made a report on 21.1.90 pointing out that appeal was out of time by 6 days and so the memo of appeal was returned to the filing Assistant Attorney-General (Civil) who received it on the same date and under such circumstances it was incumbent on the part of the petitioner to speedily prepare the application for condonation of delay and to file the same in Court. But this was not done and the memo of appeal was not filed till 20.5.90.

6. Referring to this fact the learned Advocate for the opposite parties contends that petitioner did not show due diligence in prosecuting the matter, rather it acted carelessly. It is further submitted that petitioner acted with gross negligence and had shown want of due diligence in prosecuting the matter:

7. Admittedly memo of appeal became time barred on 5.1.90 and from that date limitation started running. Thus the learned Advocate for the opposite parties urged that if period of limitation which started running from 5.1.90 be computed till the filing of the memo of appeal on 19.5.90, this period (from 5.1.90 to 19.5.90) covers 135 days :—(January 27 days, February 28 days, March 31 days, April 30 days and May 19 days, total 135 days). And from these 135 days 10 days are to be excluded as that period was taken by the stamp reporter for making report under rule 13 Chapter V part II of High Court Rules. Thus, after exclusion of time taken by the Stamp Reporter total days stands 125 days. But by the 1st application under section 5 of the Limitation Act condonation of delay of six days was sought although 125 days delay occurred and that first application was filed on 19.5.90. This fact of seeking condonation of delay of six days though delay occurred 125 days shows another act of negligence and want of due diligence.

8. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties continued to urge that when the matter relating to condonation of delay was being heard by their Lordships, the learned Assistant Attorney-General realised that the condonation of delay for the entire period was not sought for and on being conscious of this fact, the 2nd application dated 21.6.90 seeking condonation of delay of 104 days was filed when the matter was in the process of being heard but still 21 days delay remain unexplained. Referring to this fact learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that petitioner acted with gross negligence and as such prayer for condonation should not be considered.

9. I have been taken through the judgment pronounced by their Lordships as well as other materials on record. It is settled law that burden rest on the party who seeks indulgence of the Court in his favor to adduce distinct proof of sufficient cause on which he relies. It is for the appellant-petitioner to show that his conduct throughout the period between the date of impugned judgment and filing of the appeal has been of such a character that it would be proper to condone the period of delay that has occurred beyond the period of limitation and that appellant-petitioner must further explain for the delay of every day inasmuch as delay of one day may be as fatal as delay of 50 days. Therefore, every day's delay must be properly explained.

10. Limitation act does apply to the government as well as to any other citizen unless, of course, its application is excluded under some other law. In Civil matter delay in filing appeals or petition save in exceptional cases should not be lightly condoned for a valuable right has accrued to the other parties of which he cannot be deprived for any substantial reasons. To make department of the Government exception to this Rule would be putting a premium on negligence and want of proper diligence in public offices. The State in not entitled to special consideration in the matter of condoning of delay. An extension of time under section 5 of Limitation Act cannot be granted merely on the ground that the prescribed period of limitation was not sufficient so far as Government was concerned because the matter had to pass through hands of several officers. Government department should be more vigilant as Government Department is staffed with educated and paid officers but private citizen is deprived of this privilege. Section 5 of Limitation Act gives discretion to the Court in determining what is sufficient cause and that the discretion has to be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily.

<u>11. The learned Deputy Attorney General urged on behalf of the petitioner that delay was caused as the file had to pass through several offices and in that process the delay occurred. In support of his contention he has relied on the decision in AIR 1987 (SC). In that case delay of only 4 days occurred. So their Lordships took a lenient view of the matter. Another decision on which the learned Deputy Attorney-General relied is reported in BLD 1986 (AD) page 180. In that decision their Lordships observed that Government does not enjoy any special privilege and that in appropriate circumstances time may be extended to Government in the matter of filing appeal. What happened in that case is that the Munsif prior to his transfer to another station did not sign the decree but his successor signed it and in that process delay occurred which escaped the notice of the Govt. pleader. It is under this circumstances their Lordships held the circumstances that cropped up in that case was beyond the control of the party and the delay was condoned.</u>

<u>12. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that the cited decisions referred to above have no manner of application to the facts of this case and that it is patent from the facts referred above that petitioner acted negligently and there is glaring want of diligence in prosecuting the proceedings and further urged that by lapse of time valuable right has accrued to the opposite parties and such right should not be lightly taken away and that the duty of the party seeking condonation is to explain each day's delay and unless it is done, delay should not be condoned. In support of this contention the learned Advocate for opposite parties has relied on AIR 1954 Vol. 41 Patna pepsu Panjab. Their Lordships observed in the following language, "appellant was not diligent and did not take every precaution that appeal to High Court should be preferred without least delay. The delay of each day has to be explained but in this case there was delay of weeks and no explanation whatsoever forthcoming." In this case the delay was not excused. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties having relied on the decision in the case of Allhwasaya and another Vs. Mohammad Shakir reported in PLD 1958 (WP) Lahore page 959 urged that counsel's gross negligence cannot form the ground for extension of time under section 5 of the Limitation Act as negligence of the counsel is the negligence of the party because he is agent of the party. In that decision "sufficient cause" has also been sought to be interpreted. Their Lordships held "sufficient cause" means something beyond the control of the party and that in determining "sufficient cause" the Court should overlook some negligence i.e. an ordinary incident of human affairs, but gross negligence cannot be condoned. In that decision it has also been held by their Lordships that delay of each day has to be explained.</u>

<u>13. In reply to the contention the learned Deputy Attorney-General urged that delay occurred due to movement of file from one department to another department of the Government. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that their Lordships of Supreme Court of India in a decision reported in AIR 1987 Vol. 74 page 1353 observed in the following language:</u>

<u>"In fact on account of an impersonal machinery and the inherited bureaucratic methodology impugned with the note-making, file pushing, and passing of the buck ethos, delay on part of the State is less difficult to understand though more difficult to approve."</u>

<u>14. So this plea that delay occurred on account of movement of file from one department to another department does not stand to reason. The fact that delay of each day needs to be explained for getting benefit of section 5 of Limitation Act, reliance has been placed in the decision reported in the case of Sarder Amarullah Khan and another Vs. Settlement of Rehabilitation Commissioner, reported in Supreme Court Monthly Review, 1974 page 483. In that case want of the diligence was noticed by their Lordships as the petition for leave to appeal was not filed till after expiry of 11 days of receipt of copy and delay of each day having not been explained, their Lordships dismissed the petition as barred by time.</u>

15. In the instant case when 2nd application dated 31.6.90 was filed only 104 days' delay was sought to be condoned but in fact delay of 125 days occurred as referred above. Thus it is evident that delay of 21 days remained unexplained. So each day's delay having not been properly explained the petitioner cannot claim the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act. It is true that expression "sufficient cause" occurring in section 5 of Limitation Act lays down that appeal may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed when the appellant satisfied the Court that he has sufficient cause for not preferring it within prescribed period. The expression "sufficient cause" is incapable of precise definition as no hard and fast rule can be laid down as under what facts to constitute sufficient cause but consistent view of the Superior Court is that "sufficient cause" means something beyond the control of the party."

16. In the instant application for condonation of delay of 21 days has neither been sought for nor explained. Further condonation of delay has been sought on filing application on piecemeal basis. One application was filed on 19.5.90 seeking condonation of delay of 6 days and subsequently another application was filed on 21.6.90 seeking condonation of delay of 104 days. This fact shows that how much negligent and careless the petitioner was in the matter of prosecuting the appeal.

17. In my view in the present case question raised is really vital to parties and is also of importance because it raises a question of principle. Discretion to be used beyond the prescribed period of limitation is well settled. It should be judicial and not to be exercised arbitrarily and such judicial discretion must be exercised on well recognised principle. It is true that in the matter of discretion no one case can be authority for another but at the same time discretion when exercised must proceed on evidence or material which the Court can legally take notice of.

18. It is true that while considering the question of reasonable excuse or sufficient reason within the scope of proviso of section 5 of the Limitation Act good faith and due diligence are pre-requisites for a litigant to establish if he wants to rely on the principle. Even considering the matter by reference to the language of proviso "sufficient reason" must at least contemplate a reason which should be considered sufficient from the point of view of a reasonably diligent man. In order, therefore, to justify omission to make the application within the period of limitation and to make out case for condonation of delay it is incumbent on the part of the petitioner to place cogent material on record which would attract the applicability of the proviso.

<u>19. A party wishing to take advantage of section 5 of the Limitation Act must satisfy the Court that it has not been negligent and had been prosecuting the case with due diligence and care. Petitioner is under strict legal duty to furnish reasonable explanation and to show sufficient cause for condonation of delay. The question of excusing delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act has to be approached from the point of view of the petitioner's conduct. The Court has no jurisdiction to extend the time where petitioner has been negligent and inactive.</u>

20. The delay of each and every day has to be explained satisfactorily before the advantage can be taken of section 5 of the Limitation Act. Petitioner having knowledge of limitation and without sufficient cause slept over the matter and allowed the period of limitation to run out and as such the delay cannot be condoned. Where no cogent reason for delay in filing appeal beyond period of limitation is shown, appeal may be barred by time. It is up to the petitioner to show that his conduct throughout the date of impugned judgment and filing of the appeal is of such character that it would be proper to condone the period of delay that has occurred beyond the period of limitation. Where the petitioner did not peruse the appeal diligently indulgence under section 5 of Limitation Act should not be shown. In the instant case petitioner having knowledge of limitation slept over the matter and allowed the period of limitation to run out and sufficient cause having not been shown to explain the delay to file appeal in time, delay should not be condoned. Further Government Department should be more vigilant and efficient being staffed by educated and paid officers. Petitioner is not entitled to claim benefit of section 5 of Limitation Act inasmuch as 21 days as mentioned above was not explained and that by 2nd application filed on 21.6.90 condonation of the entire period of delay was not sought for and the fact of seeking of condonation of delay on piecemeal basis also shows the gross negligence committed by the petitioner in prosecuting the appeal.

21. Thus, having considered the entire materials on record, facts and circumstances referred above I am inclined to hold that the petitioner is not entitled to any indulgence under section 5 of the Limitation Act.

22. I am in agreement with the view taken by his Lordship Mr. Justice Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

End.
