parties:
Bhupati Ranjan Shome & ors ------ Appellants 
vs. 
Afizuddin Sheikh &ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
M.H. Rahman, J:- This appeal is at the instance of the pre-emptees.

2. Respondent No. 1 filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of 12'34 acres of lands of some plots of C.S. Khatian No. 19 and also for 12'21 acres of land of subordinate Khatian Nos. 2-25, 27-28 and 36 of Mouza Hemchapur. His case is-that '50 acre out of '90 acre of land of Plot No. 333 belonged to Ananda Chandra Majumder who sold the same to Krishna Kumar Dey, Kamini Kumar Dey, Jamini Kumar Dey and Nalani Kumar Dey. Krishna Kumar died without any issue leaving three brothers and widow Saudamini who jointly sold the said land to Monoroma who in her turn sold the same to Satya Charan and the latter in his turn sold the same to Bhagaban Chandra Das. Bhagaban Chandra being in possession of '50 acre in Plot No.333 sold '25 acre of land on 13th February, 1956 to pre-emptor-respondent No. 1 and his brother whose names along with others were recorded correctly in the S.A. Khatian No. 23, formerly C.S. Khatian No.19. Bhagaban Chandra sold his remaining interest, that is '25 acre, to respondent No. 1 and his brother on 23rd August 1969 and thus the respondent became a co-sharer in the holding in question and as a co-sharer and an owner of contiguous lands he was entitled to pre-empt the land sold in auction on 12th December 1969 to the pre-emptees who were strangers to the case holding. Respondent No. 1 also asserted that he had no knowledge of the auction sale till 12th February, 1967 when he heard about the sale from one Nurullah. After obtaining a certified copy of the sale certificate on 30th March, 1967 he filed the case for pre-emption on 5th April, 1967.

3. The present appellants contested the case on the ground that it was not maintainable and it was barred by limitation.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the case. The court of appeal below upheld the decision. Respondent No. 1 filed a Civil Revision Application in the High Court Division being Civil Revision No. 36 of 1983 and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division allowed the pre-emptor's prayer on 29th January, 1984.

<u>5. Leave was granted to consider whether the appellate Court eyed in considering certain documents, not marked as exhibits, for ascertaining the devolution of interest on the pre-emptor when the present petitioner had no opportunity to examine them. Leave was also granted to consider further whether the omission to mention plot in question i.e. C.S. Plot No. 333 in the Sale certificate and in the writ of delivery of possession would support the pre-emptor's plea that he had no knowledge of the sale when C.S. Plot No. 333 was a part of the total lands that were sold in auction and that sale was within the knowledge of the pre-emptor.</u>

6. At the time of the hearing of the appeal only one ground was advanced with regard to the consideration of the documents, by the appellate Court, not marked as exhibits.

7. The pre-emptor filed a registered kabala dated 13th February, 1956 (exhibit-1) which shows that he purchased a portion of the disputed plot from one Bhagaban Chandra Das. It was not disputed that the petitioner and his brother's names were recorded in the S.A. Khatian. The trial court, however, held that in the absence of the document of title of the petitioner's vendor Bhagaban Clhandra Das, the petitioner's title could not be said to have been established. The decision of the trial Court was upheld by the appellate Court.

8. On behalf of the respondent it is contended that at the appellate stage the pre-emptor filed two other registered documents showing devolution of the disputed plot by Monoroma Majumder to Satya Charan Datta and then by Satya Charan Datta to the petitioner's vendor Bhagaban Chandra Das and that respondent No. 1 also filed an application for considering those documents, but the appellate Court did not pass any order on that application and without considering the same dismissed the appeal. Respondent No. 1, however, did not place before us any paper in support of this contention.

9. From the judgment of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division it appears, however, that those documents were in the file of the case. After considering them and examining the facts and other questions relating to the matter he set aside the judgments and decrees of the courts below and allowed the Miscellaneous Case of the pre-emptor.

<u>10. In the facts and circumstances of the case even if those documents that were considered by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division are ignored then there would be sufficient evidence on record, namely, the document of purchase by the pre-emptor from Bhagaban Chandra and the S.A. Khatian where pre-emptor's and his brother's names were recorded, and the fact the pre-emptor was in possession of the suit land, for allowing the case for preemption. Hence we hold that the consideration of the documents as to the devolution of the vendor's interest on the pre-emptor did not materially affect the impugned decision. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, but without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

Ahmed Meah ------ Appellant 
vs. 
Ejahar Meah & Ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J:- This appeal by special leave arises from judgment and order dated 11 March, 1984 passed analogously in Civil Orders No. 61 and 62 of 1984 by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (Chittagong Bench) summarily rejecting two revisional applications of the appellant filed under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Facts of the case, briefly, are that landlords-respndents No. 3-10 instituted Rent Suits No. 15 and 16 of 1958 for recovery of arrear rent of 1362 B.S. against Rashida Khatun (deceased), mother of the appellant relating to two separate holdings held by said Rashida Khatun. The Suits were decreed ex-parte and the holdings were put to sale in Rent Execution Cases No. 101 and 103 of 1958 respectively. Respondent No. 1 Ejahar Meah purchased both the holdings on 20-5-58 at separate auction sales and the sales were duly confirmed.

3. Appellant filed Miscellaneous Judicial case Nos. 37 and 38 respectively of 1967 for setting aside the said sales under Section 173/174(3) of the B.T. Act on 19-4-67 on the ground that decree was obtained fraudulently and there were material irregularities and/or fraud in publishing and conducting the sale. It was also contended that there was no arrear of rent for the period in question and that respondent No. 2 father of the appellant at the instigation of appellant's step-mother managed to auction purchase the holdings collusively in the benami of respondent No. 1 who is the brother of the husband of the daughter by the previous husband of the wife of Respondent No. 2.

4. Respondent No. 1 contested the cases denying all the allegations and asserting that the applications were not maintainable and barred by limitation, that the appellant knew about the sales and that there was no material irregularity in publishing and conducting the sales.

5. The trial Court and the appellate Court concurrently found that the applications for setting aside the said finding and further held that irregularities in further held that the petitions' were not maintainable as no case had been filed by the appellant forsetting asied the decress in execution of which the impugned sales took place. The appellate Court concurred with the sales were barred by limitation. The trial Court publishing and conducting the sales could not be well-proved by the appellant. Thus the Miscellaneous Cases were dismissed and this was affirmed in appeal.

6. The High Court Division by the impugned order summarily rejected the two revisional applications filed against the judgment and order passed by the Subordinate Judge in appeal affirming those of the trial Court.

7. Leave was granted to consider the submission whether the courts below erred in failing to consider the question as to whether there was any fraud and material irregularity in publishing and conducting the sales and whether the courts below ought to have noticed Ext. 3 and 3(a) which show that there was no arrear of rent for the period in question and further whether the High Court Division erred in observing that non-consideration of the said documents was not an illegality vitiating the relevant judgment.

8. It has been noticed that there has been a concurrent finding made by the courts below that the applications for setting aside the sales (Misc. Case 37/ 67 and 38/67) are barred by limitation and this has been approved by the High Court Division. Indeed it does not appear from the impugned judgment of the High Court Division that the concurrent finding as to limitation was challenged before it on any ground. Nor does it appear that the finding as to non- maintainability of the applications also was at all challenged in the High Court Division. In view of the findings as to limitation and non-maintainability the court was not at all required to consider the applications on merit as to whether there was fraud and material irregularity in publishing and conducting the sales.

9. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, learned counsel for the appellant, has sought to contend that the courts below ought to have considered the application on merit upon which the question of limitation depends. It is difficult to follow his argument because the merit of the case could not be considered before deciding the question of limitation as that would amount to putting the cart before the horse. Mr. Chowdhury in course of his submission has stressed that Exts. 3 and 3(a) show that there was no arrear rent due and the holdings were sold at a shockingly low price. According to him the proceedings were apparently fraudulent and if fraud was found on consideration of merit of the case relief should have been granted in spite of the delay or bar of limitation as court cannot allow a fraud to stand. In support of his submission he has referred to the following decisions; 59 C.W.N. 1082, II DLR (PC) 143, 9 DLR 601 and 13 DLR 101.

10. Going through the said decisions it is found that not only the facts of the said cases are different but they also do not support Mr. Chowdhury's proposition. In the Calcutta Weekly Note case there was no question of limitation and the decision relates to interpretation of the second proviso to Order 21 Rule 90 C.P.C. This decision has relied upon a Privy Council case which is reported in 11 DLR (PC) 143. In the 9 DLR case an order of the House Rent Controller which was said to have been obtained by practicing fraud upon him was at issue. In the High Court objection to the application for review of the said order was raised, inter alia, on the ground of limitation. The learned Single Judge observed that when a fraud is committed on a Court, the Court has inherent power to set it right and no order obtained by practicing fraud on the court and on the parties should be allowed to stand on record. In the case reported in 13 DLR 101 there was an application under Order 21 Rule 90 C.P.C. for setting aside the sale on the ground that there were fraud and material irregularity in the publication and conduct of the sale. The decree-holder auction-purchaser, inter alia, pleaded the bar of limitation. The trial Court, besides other, upheld this plea but the Subordinate Judge on appeal held that the application was filed within time from the date of knowledge of the judgment-debtor and the application was thus not barred by limitation. The learned Single Judge observed on the question of limitation that in a case to have the sale set aside under Order 21 Rule 90 C.P.C on the ground of fraud in the publication and conduct of the sale, the judgment-debtor must have knowledge not merely of the fact of sale but a clear and definite knowledge of the facts which constitute the fraud before time can run against him.

<u>11. It will be seen that in the facts and circumstances of the present case the principles referred to in the said cases have no manner of application. The appellant could not prove by cogent evidence that he could not file the applications within time because of fraud or that his applications were within time from the date of his knowledge of such fraud. In the present cases the disputed sales took place on 20-5-58 and it has been found that the appellant came to know about the sales on 26-4-59 and 4-5-59 but he filed the applications for setting aside the sales in 1967. The applications being thus clearly time- barred, the courts were not obliged to consider the case on merit whether there were irregularities in conducting the sales and the holdings were sold at a shockingly low price etc. Even so the appellate Court has recorded a finding on merit also. As regards the claim that there was no arrear rent due the High Court Division rightly pointed out that in the Misc. Cases before the Executing court, the Executing court could not go behind the decree and the decrees themselves could not be challenged as fraudulent as done in the instant cases. Further it has been rightly pointed out that Ext.3 and 3(a) were not even relevant for the purpose of coming to a decision whether the sales were brought about fraudulently and thus non-consideration of those documents by the courts below could not be treated as an illegality vitiating their judgment. Mr. Chowdhury could not and as a matter of fact has not disputed the concurrent findings as to limitation and non-maintainability. That being so, it is clear that the points sought to be raised by Mr. Chowdhury cannot proceed further, rather at all.</u>

12. For the reasons stated it is found that the High Court Division committed no error in rejecting the revisional applications summarily.

Accordingly the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 42 of 1982.
lawyer:
Dewan AMS Zaman, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Nazrul Islam Chowdhury and Md. Abdur Rab, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Saifqur Rahman ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Mvi. Mazmul Hossain Khan & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker, J. : This appeal by the plaintiff-appellant is against the judgment and order dated 19.12.81 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 423 of 1981 rejecting the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code.

2. The plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for a declaration that the award dated 5.8.79 given by the defendants 1-6 and Mvi. Abdul Sattar since deceased was null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff. It has been averred in the plaint that there was a dispute between the plaintiff and his father Mvi. Abdus Sobhan, since deceased, on one hand and Ataur Rahman, his full-brother on the other hand over their paternal properties and ultimately the dispute was referred to the 7 arbitrators, defendant Nos. 1-6 and deceased Abdus Sattar for an adjudication as per terms embodied in the body of the agreement dated 30.6.79. It has been stated in the plaint that Ataur Rahman who was a wage-earner in the United Kingdom influenced the defendant No. 1 who was the Chairman, that the said defendant No. 1 turned down the prayer of the plaintiff for adducing evidence in the arbitration proceedings and that the award was, in fact, prepared by one Mr. Saiful Alam Khan, Advocate at the instance of defendant No. 1 who was influenced by the said Ataur Rahman. It has also been stated that the award was not signed by the arbitrators on 15.7.79 in presence of both the parties as has been recited in the award.

3. The defendants appeared in the suit and filed an application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code praying for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred by the provisions of Arbitration Act, 1940. It is stated in the application that the petitioner-defendants and others were appointed arbitrators by the plaintiff and others for arbitration in a dispute amongst them and the arbitrators gave their award on 5.8.79. That Ataur Rahman who was one of the parties to the arbitration, filed the award in Court under section 14 of the Arbitration Act for passing judgment and decree in terms of the award in Title Suit No. 366 of 1977. That the plaintiff filed a petition in that suit praying for analogous hearing of that suit with the present suit with the malafide intention of delaying the disposal of Title Suit No. 366 of 1977. The defendant-petitioner, therefore, submitted that the suit was not maintainable challenging the validity or otherwise of the award except in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties found that the suit was in substance for setting aside the award dated 5.8.79 and since the cause of action in the suit according to the plaintiff arose on 7.12.79 when the plaintiff came to know about the award for the first time and since the plaintiff as defendant No.2 appeared in Title Suit No. 366 of 1978 on 20.12.79 and since the present suit was instituted on 5.12.81 the suit was barred under the provisions of Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The learned Subordinate Judge after holding that the suit was barred by limitation rejected the plaint under Order 7 rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. It is submitted by Mr. Dewan AMS Zaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant, that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in holding that the suit was barred under Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The learned Advocate, however, submitted that the period of limitation for such suit was 6 years under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. But on the perusal of the application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure it is apparent that the defendant-petitioners filed the application praying for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge went beyond the pleadings and wrongly held that the suit was barred by Article 158 of the Limitation Act. The question before the Court was whether the suit was barred by law as provided in clause (d) of rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the reading of the plaint it does not appear that the suit was barred by limitation. The learned Subordinate Judge, therefore, was wrong in holding that the plaint was liable to be rejected as the suit was barred by limitation under Article 158 of the Limitation Act.

<u>6. Mr. Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondents, however, has contended that the suit was barred by section 32 of the Arbitration Act and therefore, the plaint was liable to be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Afaq Ahmed Ansari Vs. Zamir Hossain Ansari reported in PLD 1955 Sind 282 and also the case of Amin & Co. Vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 18 DLR 629.</u>

7. It appears that the parties referred their disputes for arbitration to 7 Arbitrators in accordance with the Arbitration agreement dated 30.6.79 and the arbitrators made an award on 5.8.79 and one of the parties to the arbitration agreement filed the award in Court under section 14 of the Arbitration Act for making the award the Rule of the Court for which Title Suit No. 366 of 1977 is still pending disposal. During the pendency of that suit the plaintiff instituted the present suit, namely, Title Suit No. 423 of 1981 for a declaration that the award dated 5.8.79 was illegal, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff. Section 14 of the Arbitration Act provides that when the arbitrators have made their award, the arbitrators at the request of any party to the agreement or any person claiming under such party or if so directed by the Court cause the award to be filed in Court and the Court shall thereupon give notice to the parties of the filing of the award and after hearing the parties pronounce its judgment thereon. In the present case after making the award, at the request of one of the parties, the award was filed in Court upon which Title Suit. No. 366 of 1977 was started; and during the pendency of that suit the plaintiff instituted the present suit. Section 31 of the Arbitration Act is to the following effect:

31. (1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, an award may be filed in any Court having jurisdiction in the matter to which the reference relates.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force and save as otherwise provided in this Act, all questions regarding the validity, effect or existence of an arbitration agreement between the parties to the agreement or persons claiming under them shall be decided by the Court in which the award under the agreement has been, or may be, filed and by no other Court.

(3) All applications regarding the conduct of arbitration proceedings or otherwise arising out of such proceedings shall be made to the Court where the award has been, or may be, filed, and to no other Court.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, where in any reference any application under this Act has been made in a Court competent to entertain it, that alone shall have jurisdiction over the arbitration proceedings and all subsequent applications arising out of the reference and the arbitration proceedings shall be made in that Court and in no other Court.

8. Then section 32 of the Arbitration Act laid down the bar to any suit questioning the validity of the arbitration agreement or the award, which is to the following effect:

"Notwithstanding any law for the time being in force, no suit shall lie on any ground whatsoever for a decision upon the existence, effect or validity of an arbitration agreement or award, nor shall any arbitration agreement or award be set aside, modified or in any way affected otherwise than as provided in this Act."

Then section 33 provides the remedy to any party objecting to any reference or an award. Section 33 is to the following effect:

Section 33: Any party to an arbitration agreement or any person claiming under him desiring to challenge the existence or validity of an arbitration agreement or an award or to have the effect of either determined shall apply to the Court and the Court shall decide the question on affidavits;

Provided that where the Court deems it just and expedient, it may set down the application for hearing on other evidence also, and it may pass such orders for discovery and particulars as it may do in a suit.

Provided that no application challenging the award shall be entertained by the Court unless the applicant has deposited in Court the amount which is required to pay under the award or has furnished security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum or for the fulfillment of any other objection by him under the award."

It appears that sub-section (2) of section 31 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for time being in force, all questions regarding the validity of an award shall be decided by the Court in which the award has been filed or may be filed and by no other Court. Section 32 gives the scheme of the Arbitration Act which is to prevent the parties to the arbitration agreement from agitating the question relating to arbitration in any manner other than that provided by the Act and it prohibits the filing of a suit for setting aside, amending or modifying in any wayan award. Sections 31 and 32 of the Arbitration Act bar any suit to set aside an award otherwise than as provided in the Arbitration Act itself and section 33 provides the remedy to the parties who desire to challenge the validity of an arbitration agreement or the award itself. It is under section 33 that any party to an arbitration agreement may apply to the Court for setting aside the award on the grounds as provided in section 30 of the Arbitration Act. The period of 30 days limitation provided under Article 158 of the Limitation Act is applicable to such an application for setting aside an award and the limitation starts from the date of service of notice of filing of the award in Court.

<u>9. I t has been so held in the case reported in PLD 1955 Sind 282 that once the dispute between the parties relating to any matter has been referred to arbitration, the only remedy open to the parties is under the Arbitration Act and not through any suit. The non-obstante clause in section 32 of the Arbitration Act starts with "Notwithstanding any law for the time being in force no suit shall Lie……………….."Thus once an award has been made and the award is filed in Court for making the same Rule of the Court no suit can be filed for the purpose of avoiding the award and the only remedy under the Arbitration Act to the parties is provided under section 33 of the Act. Similar view was expressed by a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court in the case reported in 18 DLR 629 as referred to above. In that case the arbitrators gave an award and it was filed in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka being Title Suit No. 8 of 1960. During the pendency of that suit one of the parties filed Title Suit No. 56 of 1962 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka praying for a declaration that the award filed in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge was void illegal and unenforceable in law. The Subordinate Judge 4th Court Dhaka after hearing the parties held that the suit was maintainable and it was not hit by section 32 of the Arbitration Act. Against that order the Dhaka High Court was moved in revision and a Division Bench made the Rule absolute holding that the suit was not maintainable.</u>

<u>10. In the case before us the plaintiff-appellant filed the suit for a declaration that the award dated 5.8.79 which was filed in Court in Title Suit No. 366 of 1977 was illegal void and not binding upon the plaintiff. The defendants thereafter filed the application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred by the provisions of Arbitration Act. Since section 32 of the Arbitration Act bars such a suit challenging the validity of an award we find that the suit was barred by the provision of section 32 of the Arbitration Act. The learned Subordinate Judge should have rejected the plaint on the finding that it was barred by the provision of section 32 of the Arbitration Act. Instead he rejected the plaint as being barred under Article 158 of the Limitation Act which is not tenable.</u>

In the result the appeal is dismissed. The judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is upheld but on different ground. There will be no order as to cost.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original order No. 171 of 1984.
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed ----- for the appellant. 
Fakir Abdul Mannan with Zakir Ahmed ----- for the respondents.
parties:
Chowdhury Saifuddin Ahmed ------ Appellant 
vs.  
Shamsuddin & Ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
MUSTAFA KAMAL. J. - This first miscellaneous appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 19.4.84 passed by Mr. Ali Ashraf Khan Lodi, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 239 of 1980 dismissing an application of the petitioner-appellant under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>2. Title Suit No. 322 of 1977 was filed by the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-8 against the appellant and others as defendants for partition of the partiable properties in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The suit was fixed for ex parte hearing on 16.7.80. The appellant being defendant No. 26 was out of the country on a visit to the U.S.A. from 25.6.80. He could not take any steps, nor could he instruct his learned Advocate. In such circumstances the suit was decreed ex parte on 16.7.80. His learned Advocate, owing to inadvertence, pursued the cause list of Title Suit No. 322 of 1980 and mistakenly noted in his diary that the title suit in question was fixed for hearing on 18.8.80 and there aft 28.9.80. When he found on 28.9.80 that the s was set down for solenama, it aroused his suspicion and so he looked for the records of Tide Suit No. 322 of 1977, but the same could not be traced and the annual vacation came about within a few days. In the meanwhile the appellant returned from U.S.A. on 7.9.80. His only son died in a road accident on 27.9.80. For full two months thereafter he was not in a mental state to take any steps in worldly affairs. After re-opening of the Court his learned Advocate traced or the records of Title Suit No. 322 of 1977 and came to learn for the first time on 20.11.80 that the suit was decreed ex parte on 16.7.80. This information was communicated to the appellant on 23.11.80. Thereafter, the appellant filed the miscellaneous case on 20.12.80. The appellant prayed that his application be registered and after hearing the parties the ex parte decree dated 16.7.80 be set aside.</u>

3. The plaintiff-respondents contested the miscellaneous case by filing a written objection in which they contended that the application was not maintainable in the present form, that it was bad for defect of parties, that it was barred by limitation and that it was made only to harass and deprive the respondents of the fruit of the decree. It was stated that the appellant entered appearance in the suit in 1977 and obtained adjournment for three years on various pretexts to file written statement. When he failed to do so, the suit was fixed for ex parte hearing and even the ex parte hearings were adjourned from time to time upon the prayer of the appellant. Finally, the suit was decreed ex parte on 16.7.80. Thereafter a Pleader Commissioner was appointed who surveyed the suit properties and submitted his report but the appellant did not file any objection and the report of the Pleader Commissioner has been accepted and final decree has been passed in the partition suit. The bonafide mistake of the learned Advocate for the appellant was not a bonafide one. The plaintiff-respondents also filed an additional written objection and contended that the appellant has no longer any locus standi to file the miscellaneous case, because he has already divested himself of his entire interest in the suit properties. The respondents also vigorously denied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing or that the delay in filing the miscellaneous case was unintentional. They contended that the ellaneous case was a malafide one and was filed with the object of harassing the respondents for unlawful gain.

4. Upon these averments the learned Subordinate Judge framed the following points for determination:-

1. Was the defendant-petitioner prevented by sufficient cause from contesting the suit?

2. Is the miscellaneous application barred by limitation?

3. Is the miscellaneous application bad for defect of parties?

4. Is the petitioner entitled to get the ex parte decree set aside as prayed for?

5. On point No. 1, the learned Subordinate Judge held in favour of the appellant. On point No. 2, the learned Subordinate Judge held that a party who intends to take the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act must file a separate petition. Since the appellant has not done so, the miscellaneous case is barrred by limitation. On point No. 3, the learned Subordinate Judge held that the miscellaneous case was filed without bringing on record the other defendants who have got shams. This is a partition suit and since the saham taking defendants have equal status of the plaintiff, the appellant ought to have made them parties under Order 9, rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the miscellaneous case is bad for defect of parties. On point No.4, the learned Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not entitled to get any relief in this case. As such, the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the miscellaneous case on contest but without any order as to costs.

6. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the defendant No. 26-appellant submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally in holding that a party who wishes to obtain the benefit of section 5 of the Limitation Act must always file a separate petition in order to be able to obtain a benefit of that section.

7. It is admitted on all hands that in the present case the appellant has stated that the suit was decreed ex parte on 16.7.80 that he left for U.S.A. on 27.6.80 and returned to the country on 7.9.80. It is also admitted that he has explained what happened from 7.9.80 to 20.12.80 when he filed the miscellaneous case. It is strongly contended by the other side, however, that the appellant's account of what happened between 7.9.80 to 20.12.80 is patchy and disjointed, but that concerns the merit of the appellant's explanation. The point to note in this case is that without filing a separate application under section 5 of the Limitation Act the appellant has sought to explain in the application under Order 9, rule 13 itself as to why he was delayed in filing the miscellaneous case within the period of limitation of 30 days from the date of passing of the ex parte decree. Ii is also clear from the evidence on record that the appellant has examined himself as P.W.1 and his learned Advocate Mr. Syed Altaf Hossain as P.W.2 and that they have sought to explain the happenings from 7.9.80 to 20.12.80 in their respective evidence. It is also on record that the plaintiff-respondents by examining one witness, O,P.W.1 Kamaluddin, have seriously disputed the appellant's contentions regarding the happenings between 7.9.80 to 20.12.80.

8. It is in the background of these peculiar facts and circumstances of the present case that Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that a formal application under section 5 of the Limitation Act is a mere matter of form and not of substance. He submits that when the cause of delay has been explained in the application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, evidence has been adduced by both parties on the same and arguments have been advanced, there remains nothing for the Court to ask for. On the basis of the averments and the evidence on record the Court can come to a conclusion whether the Court will condone the delay in filing the miscellaneous case or not. But the learned Subordinate Judge without considering the averments and the evidence on record has found the miscellaneous case to be barred by limitation simply on the ground that no formal application under section 5 of the Limitation Act has been preferred by the appellant. Mr. Ahmed submits that in the interest of justice it should be held, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, that no formal application under section 5 of the Limitation Act was necessary.

<u>9. It seems to us that although it is desirable that in all cases where a party who wishes to take advantage of section 5 of the Limitation Act ought to file a separate application for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act setting out the facts and the reasons for the delay, it is not absolutely essential, as in the present case, that a formal application must be filed as a matter of inflexible rule on am of dismissal of the main application itself. If the main application contains the entire facts or reasons for the delay, if evidence has been given both in favour and in rebuttal of the same, then there remains nothing for the Court to ask for. The door of justice will not be shut out to the party simply because a formal application is lacking.</u>

<u>10. We are supported in our view by the language of section 5 of the Limitation Act which is as follows:</u>

<u>"5. Any appeal or application for a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application to which this section may be made applicable by or under any enactment for the time being in force' may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed therefor, when the appellant or applicant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within such period."</u>

<u>The section lays stress on satisfying the Court that the appellant or applicant had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within the statutory period. It does not say that the only medium through which the Court can be satisfied is by way of a separate application. On the contrary, section 5 "may be made applicable" by or under any enactment to an appeal or application for a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application. In other words, appeals or applications stand on their own strength, but section 5 is "made applicable" to them. An appeal or application, therefore, can be preferred or made along with averments that are necessary to be made to make section 5 "applicable" to them. The section itself does not postulate making of a separate and independent application.</u>

11. This view of ours finds support in the case of Firm Kaura Mal-Vs-Firrn Mathra Dass, A.I.R. 1959 (Punjab) 646

where it is held as follows:-

"The discretion under section 5 of Limitation Act has to be a judicial discretion and not an arbitrary one. Merely because there was no written application filed by the appellant is nanny a sufficient ground for refusing him the relief, if he is otherwise entitled to it. Procedure is meant for advancing and not for obstructing the cause of justice; and if the entire material is on the record, it cannot promote the ends of justice if that material is ignored and the relief refused to the appellant, merely because he had not claimed it by means of a formal application in writing or that a formal affidavit was not filed. The language of section 5 also does not provide that an application in writing must be filed before relief under the said provision can be granted".

12. In the case of Mt. Kulsoomun Nissa and another-Vs-Noor Mohammad alias Sultan Haider and another, A.I.R. 1936 (Allahabad) 666, Sulaiman, C.J. did not approve of a dismissal of appeal as time-barred merely on the ground that the appellant had not made a formal application for extension of time under section 5 of the Limitation Act His Lordship held that the appellate Court erred in exercising its discretion in the matter.

<u>13. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case we hold that although as matter of prudence and procedure a separate application under section 5 of the Limitation Act is always desirable, no harm has been done in the present case as in the main application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellant has sought to explain the reasons of his delay in filing the miscellaneous case. He has also led evidence to that effect and the other side has also led contrary evidence. When all the materials were on record there was hardly anything left for the Court but to consider his case of condo nation of delay on merit. Of course, in his application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellant has not expressly prayed for condo nation of delay in filing the miscellaneous case, which he ought to have done, but we also waive that failure, because after all he has prayed that his "application be registered" which may be taken to be a prayer for condo nation of delay.</u>

14. We have, therefore, to consider whether on facts the appellant has been able to establish (l) that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing and (2) that' he has explained satisfactorily the delay in filing the miscellaneous case. We will deal with the first point first.

15. The appellant as P.W.1 Visa cross-examined in detail and from his cross-examination we find that he entered appearance in me suit in 1977 and he took time for more than three years to file a written statement On 23.11.79 the court granted time to me a written statement as a last chance, in default fixed the suit for ex parte hearing on 22.12.79. Thereafter the ex parte hearing was fixed on 18.2.80, 17.3;80, 17.4. 80, 27.5.80 and 16.5.80. P.W.l has admitted that on 16.6.80 he again applied for time but the prayer was rejected and 16.7.80 was fixed for ex parte disposal.

<u>16. It is the appellant's case that he left for U.S.A on 21.6.80 and, therefore could not take any steps on the date of hearing. But it is clear from his cross-examination that 16.7.80 was fixed as the date for ex parte disposal in his presence and within his knowledge. Therefore, it is pertinent to inquire as to what steps he took before he left for U.S.A. so that the hearing on 16.7.80 is taken care of. Nothing has been said to that effect in me application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In his evidence P.W.1 stated that before leaving the country he requested his Advocate to take steps for adjournment of hearing a statement which was not made in the application itself and which was rightly objected to. P.W.2, Mr. Syed Altaf Hossain learned advocate for the appellant in the trial Court does not say a word corroborating P.W.1 on this point. Therefore, we can safely come to the conclusion that the appellant left for U.S.A. without making any arrangement for conduct of the case on 16.7.80. There is nothing on record that he had to leave for U.S.A. suddenly or that he had no time to instruct his lawyer. P.W. 2 has stated that on 16.7.80 he flied an application for adjournment on the ground of his illness. No such application has been filed or marked as an exhibit and no such application is available in the case record either. P.W. 2 Mi. Syed Altar Hossain was engaged by the appellant from the beginning of the suit till the filing of the miscellaneous case and. therefore, it is absolutely unexplained as to what positive steps he took on 16.7.80 for the conduct of the case. The learned Subordinate Judge has found from the mere fact of the appellant's stay abroad that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. Mere absence from the country in the facts and circumstances of the case does not amount to a sufficient cause. In the background of the case history we are inevitably led to inquire as to whether the appellant made sufficient arrangement for conduct of the case on 16.7.80 or not. From the evidence on record we find that he did not and, therefore, we do not think mat he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing on 16.7.80. The order-sheet dated 16.7.80 does not show that his lawyer prayed for any adjournment, far less on any ground of illness and his absence on that day and the absence of his lawyer cannot be explained.</u>

17. On the second question as to whether the delay in filing the miscellanceous case should be condoned or not, we find that the petitioner returned LO the country on 7.9.80 and his only son died in an accident on 27.9.80. P.W.l says in his evidence that on return he contacted his Advocate who told him that the date of hearing was fixed sometime in the second week of September, 1980 and that he would inform the appellant the date of hearing in due time. There is no corroboration of this statement of P.W.l in the evidence of P. W.2 except that he made' a bland statement that on return to Bangladesh his client contacted him.

18. Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan, learned Advocate for the-plaintiff-respondents has rightly contended that the time between 7.9.80 to 27.9.80 has been left totally unexplained and there is no reason why the delay during the period should at all be condoned.

<u>19. P.W. 2 Mr. Syed Altaf Hossain stated in his evidence that he found the next date of hearing of the suit on 18.K80 and on 28.9.80 he found the suit fixed for compromise. He checked up the matter on 29.9.80 and found to his dismay that he was pursuing the dates of Title Suit No. 322 of 1980 instead of Title Suit No. 322 of 1977 owing to inadvertence. It passes our understanding as to why P:W. 2 thereafter went after the record of Title Suit No. 322 of 1977, when in a matter of minutes he could check up the daily cause list to find out as to what happened to the Title Suit No. 322 of 1977 on 16.7.80. We are, therefore, not convinced at all that the entire period from 28.9.80 to 20.11.80 was consumed by P.W. 2 in the wild goose chase of the records of Title Suit No. 322 of 1977. This was a convenient excuse and we cannot accept that.</u>

<u>20. Finally, P.W. 2 stated that he came to know finally on 20.11.80 after search that the suit was decreed ex parte on 16.7.80. His client, P.W.l, was informed about the ex parte decree on 23.11.80. Thereafter it has not been explained at all why the miscellaneous case was filed on 20.12.80. A non-notified co-sharer under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act files an application for pre-emption from the date of his knowledge, but a person against whom an ex parte decree has been passed cannot borrow the analogy of section 96 and take upon himself an added advantage of another 30 days to file the miscellaneous case. This part of the delay is not explained at all anywhere.</u>

21. Therefore, for all the above reasons we think that although the appellant has adduced facts and reasons in support of his prayer for condo nation of delay, he has not satisfactorily explained the causes of delay at all. His explanations are patchy and fragmented. There are large gaps here and there and no amount of explanation can plug the holes. Hence we hold that the miscellaneous case-is 'barred by limitation.

22. On the question of defect of parties we are informed that apart from the plaintiff-respondents no one else has been granted any saham by the preliminary and final decrees. As such, we do not think that the miscellaneous application was bad for defect of parties.

23. For all the above reasons, we do not find that it is a fit case for interference.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed, but in the facts and circumstances of the case we make no order as to costs.

MOHAMMAD ISMAIL UDDIN SARKER, J:  I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury, J.: This appeal filed by the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallayan Trust is directed against the judgment and order dated 19.8.90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Narayanganj in Title Suit No. 12 in Title Suit No. 12 of 1986 granting mandatory injunction against the appellant namely, Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust, defendant in the suit.

2. Facts leading to this, in short, are that the instant property which are few jute godowns at Narayanganj being Municipal Holding No. 150/152, BK Road Narayanganj is claimed by both the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust and also by Nurul Hossain, son of late Abdul Huq, the plaintiff of Title Suit No.12 of 1986 out of which the mandatory injunction arose and the subject matter of the present appeal.

3. The order of the learned court below granting mandatory injunction did not give details of the background. The appellant before this Court namely, Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Trust claimed the said property by purchase. They claim to have purchased it from the Government and hence have every right to sell and dispose of the said property as owner and the plaintiff had no reason to file the suit for declaration of their right, title and possession over the same and if they are in possession of the property it is in possession of trespassers, they having no right, title and interest in the property. It is the further case of the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust that eviction was caused by the Government in exercise of the power under Ordinance 24 or 1970 namely, the provision of law authorising the Government to take khas possession of the Government khas land by evicting trespassers. The Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust has nothing to do with the proceeding of the eviction and it is the further case of the appellant that this mandatory injunction as allowed and ordered by the Court below is misconceived because under the provision of Ordinance 24 or 1970 an appeal would lie against any order passed by the Government evicting a trespasser, which was not done.

4. The case of the plaintiff who has gone to the court in Title Suit No. 12 of 1986 is that Abdul Huq, the father of Nurul Hossain, the plaintiff in the suit was carrying on jute business in the suit premises under the name and style M/s. Huq Company" and he was a tenant under the original owners of the said jute godown which owners subsequently migrated to India after the Indo-Pak War in 1965 and the property became an enemy property and thereafter it vested upon the Additional Custodian of the Enemy Property vide Gazette Notification published on Friday, the 12th May, 1967 and the said property being Enemy Property thereafter vested in the Government as per PO 29 of 1972. Thereafter, the Government of Bangladesh vide letter dated 10.7.73 sold out in total 175 jute godowns including the suit godowns and 14 jute press houses to the Jute Trading Corporation vide registered Deed No. 19943 dated 29.6.74 and the said deed was executed on behalf of the Government by the Secretary, Ministry of Jute. M/s. Huq Company who was the tenant under the original owners continued as tenant in the said godowns and carried on business in continuation of his previous tenancy in the said premises, under the Jute Trading Corporation. The Jute Trading Corporation thereafter decided to sell the property along with other properties by tender and the tender was published in the daily newspapers. The plaintiffs decided to purchase the same and submitted quotation in April, 1981. The said quotation was opened on 14.5.81 and the plaintiff was informed vide letter dated 21.5.81 by the Jute Trading Corporation that his offer amounting to Take. 2,65,000.00 for the purchase of the schedule property in the suit, he being the highest tenderer, is accepted and he was further advised to deposit tender amount by bank draft in favour of the Jute Trading Corporation Ltd. within 15 days. The plaintiff submitted a demand draft being No. 811570 dated 28.5.81 addressing the Secretary, Jute Trading Corporation for the purchase of the property in schedule and it was received with acknowledgment return and vide letter dated 12.6.1981. M/s. Huq Company, the tenant was asked to hand over the possession of the premises to the purchaser Nurul Hossain, the plaintiff on or before 30.6.81 and the plaintiff also received the letter from the Secretary stating that the Government had been pleased to accept the offer and accordingly the ownership of the property concerned is transferred in favour of the plaintiff as the tender money is received in full and he was asked to submit a draft deed of conveyance for formal registration of the property. The plaintiff submitted a draft deed of conveyance but it could not be completed as in the meantime several organisations like Bangladesh Jute Marketing Corporation.Tute Trading Corporation Special Property (jute) Cell, etc. were merged into one Corporation namely the Bangladesh Jute Corporation. The same draft deed of conveyance is awaiting formal execution and registration and when that was the matter on 9.1.86 a news item was published in the daily Ittefaq that Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust invited tender to sell the same property along with other properties in auction fixing 20th January, 1986 as the date of opening auction of the sale of the properties. The plaintiff wrote a letter to the Deputy Secretary, Bangladesh Jute Trading Corporation as to the above publication and he also wrote a letter to the General Manager (Industry) Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust stating all fact of the plaintiffs ownership in the schedule property, requesting them not to sell the schedule property in auction. It is also the case that Bangladesh Jute Trading Corporation also issued a letter dated 16.1.86 addressed to the General Manager, Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust stating all the facts of the property and also the sale of the property by them to the plaintiff and requesting them to abstain from auctioning the property in question.

5. Having received no reply from the Mukti Judhya Kallayan Trust, the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit for a declaration of their right and possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act pending finalisation of the registration of the deed by the parties. It is in the plaint that no suit for specific performance of contract is necessary as the Government is always ready and willing to execute and register the deed in favor of the plaintiff.

6. From an examination of the order sheet of the suit it appears that after filing of .he suit, the plaintiff moved an application under Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for injunction and in that petition it was stated that defendant No.1 namely, Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust having no right to sell the property in any manner and the plaintiff being in possession has a right to protect his possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. The property being an enemy property was sold to the Jute Trading Corporation in June, 1974 by the Government and the plaintiff being already in possession as a tenant from the time of the original Hindu owners remained in possession and thereafter became the owner by purchase and was in possession as a purchaser though without a final registered sale deed. They have a right to maintain their possession and if the property is sold by auction by Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust they would suffer irreparable loss and injury and therefore, the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust and others are required to be restrained by order of temporary injunction not to proceed with the sale of the property by tender or to disturb the plaintiffs peaceful possession till the disposal of the suit. It is also stated in this application that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff and if the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 namely Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust and others are not restrained, the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury. That application after being moved an order was passed to show cause as to why Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust, the defendant in the suit, shall not be restrained by an order of temporary injunction till the disposal of the suit from transferring the suit property to anybody else or in any manner from interfering with the peaceful possession of the plaintiff.

7. The Rule however could not be heard and it was ordered that it would be heard along with the main suit and when that was the matter, it is the case of the plaintiff that suddenly on 29.6.90 without serving any notice upon them, the office and godown of the plaintiff was closed by police and a magistrate was present when the office and godown of the plaintiff was closed by the Magistrate under the order of the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj and it is the case that the Government through the Magistrate and the Deputy Commissioner illegally broke open the lock of the office and the godown of the plaintiff in the said premises and removed all furniture; papers etc. lying in the office, locking the godown and office of the plaintiff. It is the plaintiffs case that this step was taken by the Deputy Commissioner at the asking of the defendant Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust and other defendants, illegally, They evicted the plaintiff with the help of the Deputy Commissioner to make the suit infructuous and the plaintiff moved and application for addition of the Magistrate an the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj as a party in the suit and filed an application for temporary mandatory injunction praying for restoration of possession.

8. The matter was heard at length. It is the case of the defendant-appellant before the Court of first instance at the hearing of the mandatory injunction that the plaintiff is an unauthorised occupant in the suit premises having no right, title and interest in the said property but it is the Mukti Judhya Kallayan Trust who is the owner and the Government decided to evict the plaintiff as per provision of Ordinance 24 of 1970 and accordingly the Government directed the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj to evict the plaintiff from the suit property, who evicted the plaintiff with the help of the law enforcing agency in the presence of a 1st Class Magistrate.

9. It is seen that at the time of hearing of the temporary mandatory injunction neither the Deputy Commissioner nor the Magistrate, who had been added as a party and upon whom the notices were served, appeared to make any submission nor did they show any cause but it is the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust who contested the temporary mandatory injunction matter. The Court of Subordinate Judge, Narayanganj after hearing the parties passed the temporary mandatory injunction order which is the subject matter of the present appeal which is heard and disposed of by this judgment.

10. Mr. Md. Hannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant in this case submitted that the impugned order appealed against has been passed upon total misconception of law therefore it is liable to be set aside. In elaborating this point further he has submitted that the plaintiff having no prima facie case even for a temporary injunction in the absence of any document showing prima facie title of the plaintiff in the suit, the plaintiff was not entitled even to a temporary injunction and a mandatory injunction was, therefore not warranted because the plaintiff is a stranger to the suit property and even if he is in possession it was without any title or basis of right and therefore being a trespasser he is not entitled to any protection under the law against the real owner who is the Bangladesh Mutijudhya Kallyan Trust having purchased the property for valuable consideration from the Government of Bangladesh. Mr. Hannan further submitted that the instant eviction proceeding is one under the provision of section 24 of 1970 and PO 85 of 1972 which is a proceeding for recovery of the lands and buildings of the Government and local authorities, totally different from the proceedings of the suit and the matters relating to injunction and mandatory injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge without carefully considering the law applicable illegally entertained the application under Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure in an extra-ordinary manner by way of making the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj and the Magistrate concerned a party in the suit who actually evicted and passed the impugned order of mandatory injunction without invoking the provision of appeal as laid down in the special statute itself namely, Ordinance, No. 24 of 1970 and therefore, the order of mandatory injunction is without jurisdiction and ab initio void and therefore need be set aside.

11. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff respondent No.1 Nurul Hossain submitted that the suit of Nurul Hossain is a suit for a declaration that Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust and other defendants have no right to sell the property in any way and that the plaintiff is in possession and his possession need be protected under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. This possession of the plaintiff of the instant godown and office is not that of a trespasser but of a bonafide purchaser for value in good faith and the authority that sold the property is the legal owner of same and, therefore, the possession of the plaintiff in the suit property is protectable under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and dispossession or interference with the said possession of the plaintiff during the pendency of the suit is reversible by an order of temporary mandatory injunction by restoring status quo ante or rather the status quo between the parties as existed at the time of institution of the suit. According to the learned Advocate, this principle of law needs no citation. This eviction of plaintiff during the suit by the Deputy Commissioner through his Magistrate was totally unwarranted and it was done at the behest of the defendants in the suit by taking recourse to Ordinance XXIV of 1970. It was illegal and the opposite party did induce the Deputy Commissioner, who before was not even party in the suit, to evict the plaintiff claiming the property to be Government property when it was not Government property.

12. We have considered the submission of the learned Advocate in this matter. The matter was argued at great length and in minutest details by the learned Advocates and we heard them patiently because a point of law is involved in this case afecting the general public.

13. From an examination of the impugned judgment in this appeal, it is seen that the learned Subordinate Judge in his 3 pages judgment has narrated in short the pleadings of the parties in the suit and came to a finding that as to the averments made in the plaint which is yet to be decided, the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property by purchase from the Jute Trading Corporation at a price of Tk. 2,65,000.00 and he is in possession in continuation of his previous possession and is in possession at the moment by virtue of an agreement for sale and when he has paid the entire consideration money minus the registered document of sale when it is the contention of the Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallayan Trust that they have purchased the suit property from the Government and the plaintiff is in unauthorised possession as a trespasser and he was evicted in accordance with law.

14. The Court found that even under Ordinance XXIV of 1970 and PO 85/1972 there is a provision that no person though unauthorised in occupation would be evicted without a notice and the property in question admittedly became an enemy property. The Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust claims to have purchased the property from the Government so also the plaintiff which however, is a matter to be decided in the suit. The Court further found that the injunction petition where the plaintiff had prayed for an order of restraining the defendants from interfering with his possession is yet pending to be heard and when there is a show cause notice issued upon the defendants to show cause as to why they should not be restrained from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiff and in which the defendants had showed cause, the eviction of the plaintiff from the suit property amounts to a contempt of court, committed by defendant Nos. 1 and 2, The Court further found that till the matter is decided it could not be said who is the real owner and who is not the real owner but admittedly at the moment the property is not a Government property. Therefore, the plaintiff is entitled to obtain an order for maintaining status quo ante the suit and therefore, the court ordered for a mandatory injunction restoring the possession as it was between the parties at the time of the institution of the suit.

15. From an examination of the provision of Ordinance XXIV of 1970 it appears that there under persons to be evicted are persons who are unauthorisedly in possession of Government property or property of local authority. Section 3 of the Ordinance speaks of eviction of outgoing leases from land or building. Section 5 of the Ordinance speaks of eviction of an authorised occupant. It provides that if the Deputy Commissioner, on his own motion or upon enquiry, is satisfied that a person is an unauthorised occupant, he may issue, in the prescribed manner, a notice directing such person to vacate the land, building or part thereof in his occupation within a period of 30 days and if the person refuses or fails to vacate the land, building or part thereof in his occupation within the time fixed, then, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, it shall be lawful for the Deputy Commissioner to enter upon such land, building or part thereof and recover khas possession of the same by evicting such person and by demolishing and removing structures, if any, erected or built by that person.

16. The Ordinance provides for an appeal under section 10 which speaks that any person aggrieved by an order made under section 3 namely eviction of an outgoing lessee or section 4 namely, determination of lease and recovery of building in certain cases or section 5, eviction of unauthorised occupant or section 9 compensation for unauthorised occupation, may prefer an appeal to the Commissioner of the Division within 30 days of the service of the notice and the decision of the Commissioner on such appeal shall be final and no Court shall pass an order in any proceeding granting a temporary or ad-interim injunction restraining the Deputy Commissioner from taking possession of any land under the said Ordinance.

17. In this matter it is the clear assertion of the defendant Bangladesh Mukti Judhya Kallyan Trust that they had nothing to do with the eviction done during the pendency of the suit but it was done by the Government in exercise of the power under Ordinance XXIV of 1970. It was done legally and they being not party in the suit, they had not in any way interfered with the proceeding in that suit by eviction and the eviction was done legally and, therefore, there was no cause for a mandatory injunction.

18. We having considered the provision of Ordinance as mentioned before and find that even to evict an unauthorised occupant which means a person in occupation without obtaining any permission or authority from the provincial Government or the local authority concerned or of any legal document, cannot be evicted without a notice served upon him giving him 30 days time. Admittedly under the said provision there is an appeal against that order of eviction issued under sections 3, 4, 5 and other sections and the decision arrived in appeal would cause finality but in the instant case there is nothing on record to show that any such notice had been served. Therefore, it has been clearly found by the court below that this eviction of a person during the pendency of the suit even by the Government in exercise of the power under the provision of Ordinance XXIV of 1970 without any notice having been served, was totally illegal and may even amount to a contempt of Court.

<u>19. We do not find any reason to differ with that. It appears that in the instant case the plaintiff respondent is in possession of the property not as a trespasser or is in unauthorised occupation but was in possession on the basis of some documents however imperfect that document might be and could certainly claim to have his possession protected under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act or under the provision of the Specific Relief Act even without putting his title in to the picture and if dispossessed immediately before, could be put back in possession. Therefore, we do not find that the plaintiff was in unauthorised possession at the moment he was evicted by the Deputy Commissioner. He, under no stretch of imagination can be termed as an unauthorised occupant and even then the law gave him a right to be heard but that was also not done. When the law gives a power to do a thing said power needs to be exercised according to the law by following the procedure strictly and any departure from the procedure would be-an illegality. The eviction, therefore, was totally illegal and it was rightly found so by the court below.</u>

<u>20. The Court below after considering the facts of the case ordered that the possession as existed between the parties at the initiation of the suit should be restored and it would be by ordering temporary mandatory injunction, by asking a person to undo which was done during the pendency of the suit and to restore the possession as it was before.</u>

<u>21. An order of mandatory injunction is passed generally in extreme cases when the balance of convenience and inconvenience could call for it and when otherwise it would cause irreparable loss and injury to the person asking for the same and this is done to maintain status quo ante and is done by undoing what was done illegally in a pending suit changing the nature and character of the suit land and its possession and is always done to restore back the position between the parties as existed at the time of filing the suit.</u>

<u>22. This principle as narrated above has again been reiterated by their Lordships of the Appellate Division of this Court in the case of Abdul Jalil Munshi Vs. Abu Bakar Siddique, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42. In a similar matter of mandatory injunction the observation of the Appellate Division, in the case under report is as follows :</u>

<u>"If a party to a suit does an act to bring about a change in the state of things existing at the date of the suit or just prior to that date, in order to forestall a possible order of the Court, the Court may in an appropriate case, in exercise of its inherent power, require the offending party by issuing a temporary injunction in mandatory form, to restore the status quo ante. This principle is in consonance with fair administration of justice and this power of making an order of mandatory injunction on an interlocutory application, may be exercised, irrespective of the merits of the main case as it is one of the main concerns Of a Court of law to see that no one dares to interfere with the courts of Justice by presenting the Court with e fait accompli."</u>

23. The Court further observed that it is the duty of the Court to require the offending party by an appropriate order to undo that was done by altering the state of thing as existed on the date of the institution of the suit.

24. In the instant case, the suit was for protecting the possession of the plaintiff as under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and for a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to maintain possession and that his possession is protected under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and now, by dispossession the whole suit could become infructuous. Government from nowhere came in to the picture and very seriously interfered with a proceeding pending in a Court and preempted in a matter which is pending to be decided before the Court by evicting the plaintiff, which possession is the very subject-matter of the suit and after this eviction there may remain nothing for a declaration by the Court. Rightly it was found by the court that it amounts to a serious interference with the proceeding of the Court and a contempt of Court. The Court, it appears, however, did not refer this matter to this Court for any contempt proceeding, which could have been done.

25. Having found no illegality with the order passed by the Court which is appealed against, we find no substance in this appeal which is accordingly dismissed without any order as to costs.

The stay granted earlier as to the operation of the mandatory order of injunction is hereby vacated. The mandatory order of injunction comes into full effect and the restoration of possession of the plaintiff in the suit property be effected immediately by the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj himself and report compliance to the Court of Subordinate Judge concerned within 16 days of the receipt of this order.

Communicate this order at once.

End.
