full_judgment:
Rule in Civil Revision No. 9371/1991 at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner Renu Pada Chakraborty is against judgment and decree dated 9.2.1989 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Habiganj in Title Appeal No. 41 of 1986 allowing the appeal and reversing judgment and decree dated 30.9.85 passed by Munsif, Bahubal in Title Suit No. 485 of 1984.

Rule in CR No. 10039 of 1991 at the instance of petitioner Md. Ashabullah is against judgment and order dated 31.8.1987 passed by Subordinate Judge, Habiganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 1981 dismissing the appeal and affirming judgment and order dated 29.11.80 passed by Munsif Habiganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 146 of 1973 under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Opposite party No. 1 Renu Pada Chakraborty of this Rule is petitioner in the other Civil Revision No. 9371 of 1991 and opposite party No. 1 of that Rule is the petitioner of CR No. 10039 of 1991 and, as such, both the Rules are substantially between the same parties and over the self same property and, as such, both these Rules are disposed of by this judgment.

2. Petitioner of Civil Revision No. 9371 of 1991 as plaintiff filed the aforesaid Title Suit No. 485 of 1984 against opposite party No. 1 Asabullah, his son opposite party No. 2 Kurfan Ullah and others for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit land on the allegation that suit land originally belonged to Kunja Mohan Chakraborty who made a will in favour of the plaintiff and the plaintiff got the will probated and had been possessing the suit land cultivating paddy therein. His further case is, that defendant No. 1 obtained a decree for perpetual injunction against the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 148 of 1974 and thereafter he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 146 of 1973 for correction of the SA Khatian and though the said case was dismissed defendant dispossessed the plaintiff on 25th Sraban, 1390 BS.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 denying material allegations and stating that Kunja Mohan Chakraborty was a childless person and defendant No. 1 and his father used to serve said Kunja Mohan Chakraborty in various ways-and in consideration of their services Kunja Mohan Chakraborty settled suit land to the defendant No. 1 and his father allowing them to possess the same without rent for 20 years after developing the same and to pay rent of Taka one and one anna after expiry of 20 years and executed a hukumnama or permission deed in their favour embodying the said terms and since then they are in possession of the suit land by producing paddy after making substantial improvement of the suit land by cutting earth from the bank of the dighi and filling the dighi at huge cost and labour. His further case is, that title and possession of Kunja Mohan Chakraborty was extinguished in the suit property from the date of settlement of the same with defendant No. 1 and his father since Magh, 1359 BS and they have been in continuous possession of the same by producing paddy and filed Miscellaneous Case No. 146 of 1973 for correction of SA khatian as the same was wrongly recorded in the name of said Kunja Mohan Chakraborty and he has been paying rent with the Tahsil Office. His further case is, that taking advantage of his poverty as some powerful men of the locality with the help of the plaintiff attempted to dispossess him from the suit land he filed Title Suit No. 148 of 1974 in which plaintiff admitted his possession by filing written statement and he got decree in that suit on 27.11.76 for perpetual injunction and thereafter plaintiff filed a criminal case against him under sections 379 and 427 of the Penal Code on the allegation of cutting paddy and the said case was dismissed on 17.5.75 and the plaintiff has or had no title and possession in the suit land and he filed the suit with false allegations.

4. Mr. SK Sinha, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 9371 of 1991, submitted that Court of appeal below acted illegally in passing the impugned judgment and decree by setting aside the clear finding of the trial Court as to plaintiffs title in the suit property.

5. It appears from the trial Court's judgment that on consideration of deed of permission or hukumnama executed by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty in favour of opposite party No. 1 Md. Asabullah and his father Abdul Hakim on 19.2.53 it came to the conclusion that no title was created in the suit land in favour of defendant No. 1 and his father by the said permission deed Ext. 'Ka'. Trial Court on consideration of evidence of PWs and DWs further came to the conclusion that defendants dispossessed the plaintiff while he was in possession of the suit land. Trial Court further found that plaintiff acquired title in the suit property on the basis of will executed by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty in his favour.

6. Court of appeal below concurred with the trial Court as to plaintiffs acquisition of title in the properties left by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty on the basis of probated will in favour of the plaintiff. But the Court of appeal below on consideration of evidence of PWs and DWs, as well as decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1974 for perpetual injunction passed on 27.11.76 in favour of the defendant No. 1 and against the plaintiff and also on consideration of criminal Court's order dated 12.9.74 and 27.11.74 passed in paddy theft case and also in a proceeding under section 144 CrPC came to the conclusion that plaintiff failed to prove his case of possession and dispossession from the suit land. Court of appeal below further considered the document Ext. 'Ka' executed by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty on 19.2.53 in favour of defendant No. 1 and also his evidence as DW 1 that he filled up the dighi in the suit land and made the same cultivable and there is no existence of cremation ground since Magh, 1359 BS and he has been possessing the same by cultivating paddy and he did not dispossess the plaintiff against whom he got decree for perpetual injunction. Court of appeal below further considered the evidence of DW Nos. 2-5 who corroborated evidence of DW 1, Court of appeal below further considered the evidence of Advocate Commissioner DW 6 Aminul Islam who held local inspection of the suit land on 10.8.85 and did not find existence of any cremation ground in the suit land. Relying upon the same, Court of appeal below came to the conclusion that the defendant is in possession of the suit land from before the alleged date of dispossession and hence dismissed the suit and allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

7. It appears that defendant filed and proved his unregistered document written and executed in a plain sheet of paper by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty in favour of defendant No. 1 and his father Ext 'Ka', By this document Kunja Mohan Chakraborty permitted defendant No. 1 and his father to possess the suit land which is dighi and its bank for 20 years without any rent in consideration of service rendered by them to him by making the same fit for cultivation at their own cost and labour and thereafter to possess the same on payment of annual rent of Taka 1 and one Anna to him becoming absolute owner of the suit property in tenancy right, SA Khatian Ext. 'Kha' recorded the suit land in the name of Kunja Mohan Chakraborty but in column 23 thereof suit plot No. 199 having an area of 52 decimals has been shown in permissive possession of defendant No. 1 and his father Abdul Hakim and suit plot No. 201 having an area of 6 decimals has been shown as cremation ground for the use of members of the Hindu community. 2 rent receipts Ext. Kha(1) and Kha (2) show that Abdul Hakim paid rent of the suit land for some years. Aforesaid Hukumnama Ext. 'Ka' and SA Khatian Ext. 'Kha' were considered by the Court in Title Suit No. 148 of 1974 to find possession in favour of the plaintiff of that suit i.e. defendant No. 1 of the present suit between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. Finding of possession in that suit is binding upon the plaintiff. There is no non-reading and misreading of the evidence on record on the part of the Court of appeal below in setting aside the finding of possession by the trial Court. I, therefore, find no reason to interfere with the said finding of possession in the impugned judgment.

<u>8. Pertinent question in this Rule is whether plaintiff petitioner is entitled to recover possession of the suit land from the defendants as legatee under the will executed by Kunja Mohan Chakraborty and probated by him. Court of appeal below found that the defendants are in possession of the suit land cutting the bank and filling the dighi at their cost and labour and there is no existence of cremation ground in the suit land and the defendants are in possession from before the alleged date of dispossession. Since the defendant No.1 and his late father possessed the suit land after making substantial improvements being authorised under the said hukumnama or permission deed Ext 'Ka', Kunja Mohan Chakraborty, executant of the said deed, could not evict the defendants as he would have been bound by his promise made in the said deed. Due to intervention of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1951 defendant No. 1 could not acquire tenancy right under the said Kunja Mohan Chakraborty or his legatee since long before completion of 20 years all rent receiving interests were acquired and right of any owner of any land to create tenancy in favour of anyone was taken away. Under the said Ext. 'Ka' permissive possession of defendant No. 1 and his late father in the suit property would have ended on 19.2.73 and their tenancy right would have commenced from 20.2.73 had State Acquisition and Tenancy Act not intervened in the meantime. In the absence of creation of tenancy right continuance of defendants in possession of the suit land from 20.2.73 can only be adverse to the owner of the land. Plaintiff having filed the suit on 29.9.83 i.e. within 12 years from that date normally he could have recovered possession of the suit land on the basis of his title. But under the equitable principle of promissory estoppel Kunja Mohan Chakraborty and after his death plaintiff petitioner as his legatee is debarred from recovering possession from the defendants as they made substantial improvement of the suit land at their own cost and labour relying upon the assurance made by the previous owner Kunja Mohan Chakraborty. Equitable principles are the tools for mitigating the rigours of law. In this case equitable principle of estoppel as embodied in the Evidence Act debars the plaintiff petitioner from recovering possession from the defendant opposite parties though they did not acquire 'title in the suit land by adverse possession on the date of filing the suit. I, therefore, find nothing illegal in the impugned judgment in allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The Rule in Civil Revision No. 9371 of 1991 is therefore, discharged with cost.</u>

9. As to the Rule is Civil Revision No. 10039 of 1991 at the instance of Md. Ashabullah against judgment of affirmance in view of the fact already noticed in the other Rule that suit plot No. 199 was recorded in the permissive possession of the petitioner of this Rule during the SA operation when he did not acquire any tenancy right in the suit property, learned Advocate for the petitioner does not seriously press this Rule. I also do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment to interfere with the same inasmuch as concerned SA Khatian correctly recorded the .state of the land existing at the time of the SA survey operation. But that will not debar the petitioner of this Rule from mutating his name is the concerned SA Khatian on the basis of the appellate decree in his favour affirmed in the other Rule being Civil Revision No. 9371 of 1991.

In the result, the Rule being No. 10039 of 1991 is discharged without any order as to cost with the above observation.

End.

Vs.
Azizur Rahman ------ Opp. Party.
full_judgment:
1. This Rule seeks to call in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 19.12.80 passed by Subordinate Judge, Bogra in Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979.

2. Facts giving rise to this application may briefly be stated thus. The petitioners figuring as plaintiffs instituted a partition suit being T.S. No. 60 of 1960 in, the court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra in which opposite-party Azizur Rahman Pramanik figured as defendant No. 20. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on contest against all except defendant No. 20 against whom an ex-parte decree was passed. Being aggrieved by ex-parte dceree opposite-party (defendant) Azizur Rahman Pramanik filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979 in which petitioners were impleaded as opposite party. Opposite-party Azizur Rahman sought to have preliminary decree set aside on the ground that summons was not served on him and that it was suppressed in collusion with the process server. Learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence and other the materials on record held that summons on opposite party Azizur Rahman Pramanik who figured as defendant No. 20 in the original partition suit was not served and on this finding he allowed the application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and had set aside the preliminary decree. Petitioners being aggrieved by the order allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979 moved revisional jurisdiction of this court by filing an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

3. It appears from the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge that the summons meant for defendant-opposite party Azizur Rahman Pramanik (Defendant No. 20 in the original suit) was received by defendant No. 19 Kasimuddin Pramanik on behalf of defendant No. 20. But no evidence was led, to prove defendant 19 Kasimuddin to be the authorised agent of the opposite party defendant No. 20 and so the learned Subordinate Judge held that Kasimuddin (defendant No. 19) being not an authorised agent of defendant No. 20 defendant No. 20 was not competent to receive summons on behalf of opposite-party defendant No. 20 and on that ground learned Subordinate Judge held that service of summons on opposite party was not effected in accordance with law and on that finding he allowed the miscellaneous case and set aside the ex-parte preliminary decree passed in the original suit against opposite party Azizur Rahman.

4. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that though evidence showing Kasimuddin (Defendant No.19) as an authorised agent of defendant opposite party is lacking, this service can be deemed to be proper and valid service in view of the fact that Kasimuddin who received the summons on behalf of opposite-party happens to be the adult male member of his family. In order to support this contention reliance has been placed on the provision laid down under Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which speaks that service effected on adult member of defendant's family in absence of defendant from his residence when the service of summons sought to be effected such service shall be deemed to have been effected properly. It is further argued by the learned counsel that defendant No. 19 who received summons meant for defendant-opposite party, happens to be the adult member of the same family and as such the provision of Order 5, rule 15 is attracted to the facts of this case.

5. In repelling the contention urged by the learned counsel for the petitioner, it is submitted by the learned counsel for opposite party that provision contained in Order 5, rule 13 can not have any application to the facts of the case inasmuch as there is no evidence whatsoever to show that Kasimuddin was the adult member of opposite party’s family. It is further urged that summons meant for opposite party was served on Kasimuddin allegedly treating him to be adult male member of opposite party's family during absence of opposite party from his residence, but no evidence has been led to substantiate this plea. To prove this plea best evidence would have been that of process-server concerned but he has not been examined in this case as witness. Thus in absence of any witness supporting service of summons in the manner alleged, aid of Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked. No such plea was set up in the written objection filed in the original miscellaneous case and that ends of justice demands strict proof of service of summons in accordance with law. In support of this contention learned counsel relied on the decision reported in 36 D.L.R. 260. This decision lends unqualified support to his contention and I fully agree with the principle enunciated by his Lordship in the said decision. In elaborating his argument the learned counsel submitted that service of summons on a brother in absence of another brother will not be deemed to be a proper service unless it is proved affirmatively that brother on whom service is effected is authorised agent of the absentee brother. In order to back this contention decision reported In 21 D.L.R. 747 has been referred and relied upon. The learned counsel continued to urge that the expression "family" occurring in rule 15, Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure connotes parents and their children and no adult members of the family. To support this contention the decision in the case of Amin Khan Vs. University of Sind reported in P L.D. 899 has been relied upon.

<u>6. Heard the learned counsel of both the sides and perused the judgment pronounced by the trial court. I am of opinion that the contention urged by the learned counsel for the opposite party has much substance in it. Nowhere within four corners of written objection filed in the miscellaneous case, it has been asserted that Kasimuddin who received summons meant for opposite party defendant No. 20 is the adult member of the opposite party's family. Farther, the process server who effected service has not been examined in this case to prove that he treated defendant No.19 Kasimuddin to be the adult family member of opposite party defendant No. 20 and accordingly effected the service of summons on him, nor there Is any evidence to prove that Kasimuddin was the authorised agent of defendant No. 20 (opposite party).</u>

<u>7. In order to prove service of summons as per provision contained in Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure two conditions must be satisfied; (1) absence must be from residence; (2) if defendant is not found at his residence and there is no agent empowered to accept summons, an enquiry has to be made to find out absentee defendant's adult male member residing with defendant and in process server's affidavit, these facts must be stated. Since process server concerned has not been examined nor service return of the summons has been made exhibit, question whether aforesaid conditions stand satisfied or not does not arise for consideration. There is absolutely no evidence to show that Kasimuddin on whom the summons meant for opposite party defendant No. 20 was served, happens to be the male member of the opposite party's family and residing with him.</u>

8. The learned counsel for the opposite party has rightly submitted that the provision of law relating to service of summons should strictly be followed. Propriety of the decision cited is support of this contention, cannot be doubted. In fact every defendant in a suit has right to contest the claim of his adversary. A defendant being party to a suit has a right to be served with a summons in accordance with law.

9. Since it has been found that provision contained in Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no application to the facts and circumstances of the case, no relief can be claimed by the petitioner relying on that provision. The learned counsel for the petitioner in the last resort submitted that petitioners who figured as opposite party in the original miscellaneous case did not get a chance to contest it because of the fact that their senior lawyer being engaged elsewhere did not appear and produce any evidence. But the trial court in his judgment did not mention anything about this matter. Be that as it may, consideration of the matter on compassionate ground cannot be allowed to supersede the mandatory provision of law. Law in this regard enjoins that service of summons on defendant is to be proved strictly according to law and if proof is lacking in this regard mercy or plea of ends of justice cannot come in rescue of the aggrieved party.

10. Thus having considered materials on record and regard being had to the facts, circumstances and legal and factual aspects of the matter I am of the opinion that learned Subordinate Judge held correctly that summons in this case was not served upon defendant opposite party in accordance with law and as such no interference in the matter is called for.

In the result, this Rule is discharged with cost.

End.
